author: charles-h-spurgeon
fields.title: All of Grace
fields.subtitle: An Earnest Word to Those Seeking Salvation
fields.description: All of Grace is Charles Spurgeon’s plain and earnest presentation of the gospel, written for the reader who longs to be saved but does not know where to begin. Step by step he shows that God justifies the ungodly, that salvation is by grace through faith and not by works, and that repentance and faith are themselves God’s gifts. Warm, direct, and rich in homely illustration, it presses one invitation: come to Christ just as you are.

fields.title: To You
fields.body_html:
THE ONE WHO SPOKE and wrote this message will be bitterly disappointed if it does not lead many people to the Lord Jesus. It goes out in childlike dependence on the power of God the Holy Ghost, that He may use it to convert millions, if He so pleases. No doubt many poor men and women will pick up this little book, and the Lord will visit them with grace. With that aim in view, I have chosen the plainest language I could, and used many homely expressions. But if people of wealth and rank should glance at this book, the Holy Ghost can make His mark on them too; for what the unschooled can understand is no less attractive to the educated. Oh, that some who read it may become great winners of souls!

Who knows how many will find their way to peace through what they read here? A more important question for you, dear reader, is this — will you be one of them?

A certain man set up a drinking fountain by the roadside and hung a cup beside it on a little chain. Some time later he was told that a great art critic had found a lot of fault with its design. “But,” he said, “do many thirsty people drink from it?” Then they told him that thousands of poor people — men, women and children — quenched their thirst at that fountain. He smiled and said that the critic’s remark troubled him very little; he only hoped that on some sweltering summer day the critic himself might fill the cup, be refreshed, and praise the name of the Lord.

Here is my fountain, and here is my cup. Find fault if you like; but do drink the water of life. That is all I care about. I would rather bless the soul of the poorest street-sweeper or rag-collector than please a prince of the royal blood and fail to bring him to God.

Reader, are you serious about reading these pages? If so, we agree from the start; but nothing less than your finding Christ and Heaven is what this book is aiming at. Oh, that we may seek this together! I do my part by dedicating this little book with prayer. Won’t you join me by looking up to God and asking Him to bless you while you read? Providence has put these pages in your path, you have a little spare time to read them, and you feel willing to give them your attention. These are good signs. Who knows whether the appointed time of blessing has come for you? In any case, “The Holy Ghost saith, Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”

fields.title: What Are We At?
fields.body_html:
I ONCE HEARD A STORY — I think it came from the North of England. A minister went to call on a poor woman, meaning to give her some help, because he knew she was very poor. With his money in his hand, he knocked at the door; but she did not answer. He decided she was not at home and went on his way. A little later he met her at church and told her he had remembered her need: “I called at your house and knocked several times, but I suppose you were out, because nobody answered.” “What time did you call, sir?” “It was about noon.” “Oh dear,” she said, “I heard you, sir, and I’m so sorry I didn’t answer; but I thought it was the man come for the rent.” Many a poor woman knows exactly what that means. Now, I want to be heard, and so I want to say that I am not calling for the rent. In fact, the purpose of this book is not to ask anything of you at all, but to tell you that salvation is all of grace — which means free, gratis, for nothing.

Very often, when we are eager to get someone’s attention, our listener thinks, “Ah! Now I’m going to be told my duty. This is the man come to collect what is owed to God, and I’m sure I have nothing to pay with. I won’t be at home.” No, this book has not come to make a demand on you, but to bring you something. We are not going to talk about law and duty and punishment, but about love and goodness and forgiveness and mercy and eternal life. So do not act as if you were not at home; do not turn a deaf ear or a careless heart. I am asking nothing of you, either in the name of God or of man. I have no intention of requiring anything from you. I come in God’s name to bring you a free gift — one that will be your present and eternal joy to receive. Open the door and let my pleading come in. “Come now, and let us reason together.” The Lord Himself invites you to talk with Him about your immediate and endless happiness, and He would not have done so if He did not mean you well. Do not turn away the Lord Jesus, who is knocking at your door; for He knocks with a hand that was nailed to the tree for people just like you. Since His one and only aim is your good, lend Him your ear and come to Him. Listen carefully, and let the good word sink into your soul. It may be that the hour has come when you will begin that new life which is the beginning of heaven. Faith cometh by hearing, and reading is a kind of hearing: faith may come to you while you are reading this book. Why not? O blessed Spirit of all grace, make it so!

fields.title: God Justifieth the Ungodly
fields.body_html:
THIS MESSAGE is for you. You will find the text in the Epistle to the Romans, in the fourth chapter and the fifth verse:

“To him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.”

I want to draw your attention to these words: “Him that justifieth the ungodly.” They strike me as very wonderful words.

Are you not surprised to find an expression like that in the Bible — “That justifieth the ungodly”? I have heard that people who hate the doctrines of the cross bring this as an accusation against God: that He saves wicked men and welcomes to Himself the vilest of the vile. See how this Scripture accepts the accusation and states it plainly! Through the mouth of His servant Paul, by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost, He takes for Himself the title “Him that justifieth the ungodly.” He makes the unjust just, forgives those who deserve to be punished, and shows favour to those who deserve none. You thought, didn’t you, that salvation was for the good? That God’s grace was for the pure and holy, who are free from sin? It has settled in your mind that if you were excellent, God would reward you; and you have concluded that because you are not worthy, there could be no way for you to enjoy His favour. You must be rather surprised to read a text like this: “Him that justifieth the ungodly.” I am not surprised that you are surprised; for with all my familiarity with the great grace of God, I never stop wondering at it. It does sound astonishing, doesn’t it, that a holy God could justify an unholy man? We, with the natural legalism of our hearts, are always talking about our own goodness and our own worthiness, and we stubbornly insist that there must be something in us to win God’s notice. But God, who sees through every deception, knows there is no goodness in us at all. He says that “there is none righteous, no not one.” He knows that “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.” So the Lord Jesus did not come into the world looking for goodness and righteousness to take along with Him; He came to give them to people who have none. He comes, not because we are just, but to make us just: he justifieth the ungodly.

When a lawyer comes into court, if he is an honest man, he wants to plead the case of an innocent person and clear him before the court of the false charges brought against him. The lawyer’s aim should be to justify the innocent, and he should not try to shield the guilty. It is not within man’s right, or man’s power, truly to justify the guilty. That is a miracle reserved for the Lord alone. God, the infinitely just Sovereign, knows that there is not a just man upon earth that doeth good and sinneth not. And so, in the infinite sovereignty of His divine nature and the splendour of His indescribable love, He takes on the task — not so much of justifying the just as of justifying the ungodly. God has devised a way to make the ungodly man stand justly accepted before Him. He has set up a system by which, with perfect justice, He can treat the guilty as if he had been free from offence all his life — yes, as if he were entirely free from sin. He justifieth the ungodly.

Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. It is a truly astonishing thing — something to marvel at most of all for those who enjoy it. I know that, to this very day, the greatest wonder I have ever heard of is that God should justify me. Apart from His almighty love, I feel myself to be a lump of unworthiness, a mass of corruption, a heap of sin. I know with full assurance that I am justified by faith which is in Christ Jesus, treated as if I had been perfectly just, and made an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ; and yet by nature I must take my place among the worst of sinners. I, who deserve nothing at all, am treated as if I deserved everything. I am loved as much as if I had always been godly, when in fact I used to be ungodly. Who could help being astonished at this? Gratitude for such kindness comes dressed in robes of wonder.

Now, astonishing as this is, I want you to notice how it brings the gospel within reach of you and me. If God justifieth the ungodly, then, dear friend, He can justify you. Isn’t that exactly the kind of person you are? If you are unconverted at this moment, it describes you perfectly. You have lived without God; you have been the opposite of godly; in a word, you have been — and still are — ungodly. Perhaps you have not even gone to a place of worship on Sunday, but have lived with no regard for God’s day, or His house, or His Word. That proves you have been ungodly. Sadder still, you may even have tried to doubt that God exists, and gone so far as to say so. You have lived on this beautiful earth, full of the signs of God’s presence, and all the while you have shut your eyes to the clear evidence of His power and Godhead. You have lived as if there were no God. In fact, you would have been very glad if you could have proved to yourself beyond doubt that there was no God at all. Perhaps you have lived this way for a great many years, so that you are now well settled in your ways — and God is not in any of them. If you were labelled

UNGODLY

it would describe you as well as labelling the sea “salt water.” Wouldn’t it?

Perhaps you are a different sort of person. You have regularly kept up all the outward forms of religion, yet your heart has never been in them, and you have really been ungodly. Though you meet with the people of God, you have never met with God for yourself. You have sung in the choir, yet never praised the Lord with your heart. You have lived without any love for God in your heart, or any regard for His commands in your life. Well, you are exactly the kind of person this gospel is sent to — the gospel which says that God justifieth the ungodly. It is very wonderful, and happily it is within your reach. It suits you exactly, doesn’t it? How I wish you would accept it! If you are a sensible person, you will see the remarkable grace of God in providing for people like you, and you will say to yourself, “Justify the ungodly! Then why shouldn’t I be justified — and justified at once?”

Notice further that it has to be this way — that God’s salvation is for those who do not deserve it and have done nothing to prepare for it. It makes sense that the Bible should say so; for, dear friend, nobody needs justifying except those who have no justification of their own. If any of my readers are perfectly righteous, they need no justifying. You feel you are doing your duty well and are almost putting heaven in your debt. What do you want with a Saviour, or with mercy? What do you want with justification? You will be tired of my book by now, because it will hold no interest for you.

If any of you are giving yourselves such proud airs, listen to me for a little while. As sure as you are alive, you will be lost. You righteous people, whose righteousness is all your own work, are either deceivers or deceived; for the Scripture cannot lie, and it says plainly, “There is none righteous, no, not one.” In any case, I have no gospel to preach to the self-righteous — not a word of it. Jesus Christ Himself came not to call the righteous, and I am not going to do what He did not do. If I called you, you would not come; so I will not call you as that kind of person. No, I urge you instead to look at that righteousness of yours until you see what a delusion it is. It is not half as solid as a cobweb. Be done with it! Run from it! Oh, believe that the only people who can need justification are those who are not just in themselves! They need something done for them to make them just before the judgment seat of God. You may be sure the Lord only does what is needed. Infinite wisdom never attempts the unnecessary. Jesus never takes on what is superfluous. Making the just man just is no work for God — that would be a fool’s labour. But making the unjust man just — that is work for infinite love and mercy. To justify the ungodly — this is a miracle worthy of a God. And it most certainly is so.

Now look. If somewhere in the world there is a doctor who has discovered sure and precious remedies, who is that doctor sent to? To people who are perfectly healthy? I don’t think so. Put him in a district where there are no sick people, and he feels he is in the wrong place. There is nothing for him to do. “The whole have no need of a physician, but they that are sick.” Is it not just as clear that the great remedies of grace and redemption are for those who are sick in soul? They cannot be for the healthy, because they would be of no use to them. If you, dear friend, feel that you are spiritually sick, the Physician has come into the world for you. If you are completely ruined because of your sin, you are the very person the plan of salvation has in view. I tell you, the Lord of love had people just like you in His eye when He arranged the system of grace. Suppose a generous-hearted man decided to forgive everyone who owed him money. Clearly that can only apply to people who really are in his debt. One person owes him a thousand pounds; another owes him fifty; each needs only to have his bill marked “paid,” and the debt is wiped out. But even the most generous person cannot forgive the debts of people who owe him nothing. Not even Omnipotence can forgive where there is no sin. So pardon cannot be for you who have no sin. Pardon must be for the guilty. Forgiveness must be for the sinful. It would be absurd to talk of forgiving those who need no forgiveness — of pardoning those who have never done wrong.

Do you think you must be lost because you are a sinner? That is the very reason you can be saved. Because you admit that you are a sinner, I want to encourage you to believe that grace is appointed for people like you. One of our hymn-writers even dared to say:

A sinner is a sacred thing;
The Holy Ghost hath made him so.

It is really true that Jesus seeks and saves that which is lost. He died and made a real atonement for real sinners. When people are not playing with words, or calling themselves “miserable sinners” merely as a polite formality, I am overjoyed to meet them. I would gladly talk all night with genuine sinners. The inn of mercy never shuts its doors on them, weekday or Sunday. Our Lord Jesus did not die for imaginary sins; His heart’s blood was poured out to wash away deep crimson stains that nothing else can remove.

The black sinner — he is the very kind of man Jesus Christ came to make white. A gospel preacher once preached a sermon on the text, “Now also the axe is laid to the root of the trees,” and he preached it in such a way that one of his hearers said to him, “Anyone would think you had been preaching to criminals. That sermon should have been preached in the county jail.” “Oh no,” said the good man, “if I were preaching in the county jail, I would not preach from that text. There I would preach, ‘This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.’” Exactly. The law is for the self-righteous, to humble their pride; the gospel is for the lost, to take away their despair.

If you are not lost, what do you want with a Saviour? Should the shepherd go looking for sheep that never strayed? Why should the woman sweep her house for coins that were never out of her purse? No — medicine is for the diseased; the gift of life is for the dead; pardon is for the guilty; freedom is for those who are bound; the opening of eyes is for those who are blind. How can you account for the Saviour, and His death on the cross, and the gospel of pardon, unless men are guilty and deserve condemnation? The sinner is the gospel’s reason for existing. You, my friend, to whom this word now comes — if you are undeserving, ill-deserving, hell-deserving, you are exactly the kind of person the gospel was appointed, arranged and proclaimed for. God justifieth the ungodly.

I would like to make this very plain. I hope I have done so already; but however plain it is, only the Lord can make a person see it. At first it seems utterly amazing to an awakened man that salvation should really be for him as a lost and guilty person. He thinks it must be for him as a repentant person, forgetting that his repentance is part of his salvation. “Oh,” he says, “but I must be this and that.” All of that is true, for he will become this and that as a result of salvation; but salvation comes to him before he has any of its results. In fact, it comes to him while he deserves only this bare, beggarly, base, abominable description: “ungodly.” That is all he is when God’s gospel comes to justify him.

So may I urge anyone who has nothing good about them — who fears they do not even have a good feeling, or anything at all to recommend them to God — to believe firmly that our gracious God is able and willing to take them without anything to recommend them, and to forgive them freely, not because they are good, but because He is good? Does He not make His sun shine on the evil as well as on the good? Does He not give fruitful seasons, and send rain and sunshine in their time on the most ungodly nations? Yes, even Sodom had its sun, and Gomorrah had its dew. Oh friend, the great grace of God goes beyond anything you or I can imagine, and I want you to think of it as it deserves! As high as the heavens are above the earth, so high are God’s thoughts above our thoughts. He can abundantly pardon. Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners: forgiveness is for the guilty.

Do not try to touch yourself up and make yourself into something other than you really are; come as you are to Him who justifies the ungodly. Not long ago a great artist was painting a group of the city council in the town where he lived, and for historical reasons he wanted to include in his picture certain characters well known in the town. There was a street-sweeper — unkempt, ragged, filthy — whom everybody knew, and there was a suitable place for him in the picture. The artist said to this ragged, rough fellow, “I’ll pay you well if you will come to my studio and let me paint your portrait.” He came round in the morning, but he was soon sent packing; for he had washed his face, combed his hair, and put on a respectable suit of clothes. He was wanted as a beggar, and was not invited in any other role. In the same way, the gospel will welcome you into its halls if you come as a sinner, but not otherwise. Do not wait to reform yourself; come at once for salvation. God justifieth the ungodly, and that takes you up right where you are now: it meets you in your worst condition.

Come in your everyday rags. I mean, come to your heavenly Father in all your sin and sinfulness. Come to Jesus just as you are — leprous, filthy, naked, fit neither to live nor to die. Come, you who are the very sweepings of creation; come, though you hardly dare hope for anything but death. Come, though despair is brooding over you, pressing on your chest like a horrible nightmare. Come and ask the Lord to justify one more ungodly person. Why shouldn’t He? Come, for this great mercy of God is meant for people like you. I put it in the words of the text, and I cannot put it more strongly: the Lord God Himself takes this gracious title, “Him that justifieth the ungodly.” He makes just, and causes to be treated as just, those who by nature are ungodly. Isn’t that a wonderful word for you? Reader, do not put this off until you have carefully thought the matter over.

If any of you are giving yourselves such proud airs, listen to me for a little while. As sure as you are alive, you will be lost. You righteous people, whose righteousness is all your own work, are either deceivers or deceived; for the Scripture cannot lie, and it says plainly, “There is none righteous, no, not one.” In any case, I have no gospel to preach to the self-righteous — not a word of it. Jesus Christ Himself came not to call the righteous, and I am not going to do what He did not do. If I called you, you would not come; so I will not call you as that kind of person. No, I urge you instead to look at that righteousness of yours until you see what a delusion it is. It is not half as solid as a cobweb. Be done with it! Run from it! Oh, believe that the only people who can need justification are those who are not just in themselves! They need something done for them to make them just before the judgment seat of God. You may be sure the Lord only does what is needed. Infinite wisdom never attempts the unnecessary. Jesus never takes on what is superfluous. Making the just man just is no work for God — that would be a fool’s labour. But making the unjust man just — that is work for infinite love and mercy. To justify the ungodly — this is a miracle worthy of a God. And it most certainly is so. Now look. If somewhere in the world there is a doctor who has discovered sure and precious remedies, who is that doctor sent to? To people who are perfectly healthy? I don’t think so. Put him in a district where there are no sick people, and he feels he is in the wrong place. There is nothing for him to do. “The whole have no need of a physician, but they that are sick.” Is it not just as clear that the great remedies of grace and redemption are for those who are sick in soul? They cannot be for the healthy, because they would be of no use to them. If you, dear friend, feel that you are spiritually sick, the Physician has come into the world for you. If you are completely ruined because of your sin, you are the very person the plan of salvation has in view. I tell you, the Lord of love had people just like you in His eye when He arranged the system of grace. Suppose a generous-hearted man decided to forgive everyone who owed him money. Clearly that can only apply to people who really are in his debt. One person owes him a thousand pounds; another owes him fifty; each needs only to have his bill marked “paid,” and the debt is wiped out. But even the most generous person cannot forgive the debts of people who owe him nothing. Not even Omnipotence can forgive where there is no sin. So pardon cannot be for you who have no sin. Pardon must be for the guilty. Forgiveness must be for the sinful. It would be absurd to talk of forgiving those who need no forgiveness — of pardoning those who have never done wrong. Yes, even Sodom had its sun, and Gomorrah had its dew. Oh friend, the great grace of God goes beyond anything you or I can imagine, and I want you to think of it as it deserves! Do not try to touch yourself up and make yourself into something other than you really are; come as you are to Him who justifies the ungodly. Not long ago a great artist was painting a group of the city council in the town where he lived, and for historical reasons he wanted to include in his picture certain characters well known in the town. There was a street-sweeper — unkempt, ragged, filthy — whom everybody knew, and there was a suitable place for him in the picture. The artist said to this ragged, rough fellow, “I’ll pay you well if you will come to my studio and let me paint your portrait.” He came round in the morning, but he was soon sent packing; for he had washed his face, combed his hair, and put on a respectable suit of clothes. He was wanted as a beggar, and was not invited in any other role. In the same way, the gospel will welcome you into its halls if you come as a sinner, but not otherwise. Come, you who are the very sweepings of creation; come, though you hardly dare hope for anything but death. fields.title: It Is God That Justifieth
fields.body_html:
Romans 8:33

WHAT A WONDERFUL THING it is to be justified, or made just! If we had never broken God’s laws, we would not have needed it, because we would have been just in ourselves. A person who has done all his life the things he ought to have done, and has never done anything he ought not to have done, is justified by the law. But you, dear reader, are not that kind of person — I am quite sure of it. You are too honest to pretend to be without sin, and so you need to be justified.

Now, if you justify yourself, you will simply be deceiving yourself. So do not try it. It is never worth it.

If you ask your fellow mortals to justify you, what can they do? You can get some of them to speak well of you in return for small favours, and others will run you down behind your back for even less. Their judgment is not worth much.

Our text says, “It is God that justifieth,” and that is far more to the point. It is an astonishing fact, and one we ought to think about carefully. Come and see.

In the first place, nobody but God would ever have thought of justifying the guilty. They have lived in open rebellion; they have done evil with both hands; they have gone from bad to worse. They have turned back to sin even after they suffered for it and were forced to give it up for a while. They have broken the law and trampled on the gospel. They have refused the offers of mercy and gone on stubbornly in ungodliness. How can they be forgiven and justified? Their fellow men give up on them and say, “They are hopeless cases.” Even Christians look at them with sorrow rather than hope. But their God does not. In the splendour of His electing grace He chose some of them before the foundation of the world, and He will not rest until He has justified them and made them accepted in the Beloved. Is it not written, “Whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified”? So you see, there are some whom the Lord is determined to justify. Why shouldn’t you and I be among them?

Nobody but God would ever have thought of justifying me. I am a wonder to myself. I have no doubt that grace shows itself just as clearly in others. Look at Saul of Tarsus, who foamed at the mouth against God’s servants. Like a hungry wolf, he tore at the lambs and the sheep on every side; and yet God struck him down on the road to Damascus, changed his heart, and justified him so completely that before long this man became the greatest preacher of justification by faith who ever lived. He must often have marvelled that he was justified by faith in Christ Jesus, for he had once been a determined champion of salvation by the works of the law. Nobody but God would ever have thought of justifying a man like Saul the persecutor; but the Lord God is glorious in grace.

But even if someone had thought of justifying the ungodly, nobody but God could have done it. No one can possibly forgive offences that were not committed against himself. Suppose someone has done you a great wrong. You can forgive him, and I hope you will; but no third person can forgive him on your behalf. If the wrong was done to you, the pardon must come from you. If we have sinned against God, it is within God’s power to forgive, because the sin is against Him. That is why David says in the fifty-first Psalm, “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight”; for then God, against whom the offence was committed, can put the offence away. What we owe to God, our great Creator can cancel if it pleases Him; and if He cancels it, it is cancelled. Nobody but the great God, against whom we have sinned, can blot out that sin. So let us make sure we go to Him and seek mercy from His hands. Let us not be led astray by those who want us to confess to them; they have no authority in the Word of God for their claims. But even if they were appointed to pronounce absolution in God’s name, it would still be better to go ourselves to the great Lord through Jesus Christ, the Mediator, and seek and find pardon from His hand, since we are sure that this is the right way. Religion by proxy is far too risky. You had better see to the affairs of your soul yourself, and leave them in no one else’s hands.

Only God can justify the ungodly; but He can do it perfectly. He throws our sins behind His back; He blots them out; He says that though they be sought for, they shall not be found. With no reason for it except His own infinite goodness, He has prepared a glorious way by which He can make scarlet sins as white as snow and remove our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west. He says, “I will not remember your sins.” He goes so far as to make an end of sin. A prophet of old cried out in amazement, “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy” (Micah 7:18).

We are not talking now about justice, or about God dealing with people as they deserve. If you claim to deal with the righteous Lord on the terms of the law, everlasting wrath hangs over you, because that is what you deserve. Blessed be His name, He has not dealt with us after our sins. Instead He now deals with us on terms of free grace and infinite compassion, and He says, “I will receive you graciously, and love you freely.” Believe it, because it is certainly true that the great God is able to treat the guilty with abundant mercy — yes, He is able to treat the ungodly as if they had always been godly. Read the parable of the prodigal son carefully, and see how the forgiving father welcomed the returning wanderer with as much love as if he had never gone away and never defiled himself with prostitutes. He went so far with this that the elder brother began to grumble about it; but the father never took back his love. Oh my brother, however guilty you may be, if you will only come back to your God and Father, He will treat you as if you had never done wrong! He will regard you as just and deal with you accordingly. What do you say to that?

Don’t you see — and I want to bring this out clearly, because it is such a splendid thing — that although nobody but God would think of justifying the ungodly, and nobody but God could do it, the Lord can do it? See how the apostle throws down the challenge: “Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth.” If God has justified a person, it is well done, rightly done, justly done, and done for ever. I read a statement in a magazine full of venom against the gospel and those who preach it, saying that we hold some sort of theory by which we imagine sin can be removed from people. We hold no theory; we announce a fact. The grandest fact under heaven is this: that Christ by His precious blood really does put away sin, and that God, for Christ’s sake, dealing with people on terms of divine mercy, forgives the guilty and justifies them — not because of anything He sees in them, or foresees will be in them, but according to the riches of His mercy that are in His own heart. This we have preached, we do preach, and we will preach as long as we live. “It is God that justifieth” — that justifieth the ungodly. He is not ashamed to do it, and we are not ashamed to preach it.

The justification that comes from God Himself must be beyond all question. If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me? If the highest court in the universe has declared me just, who shall lay anything to my charge? Justification from God is a full answer to an awakened conscience. By it the Holy Spirit breathes peace over our whole nature, and we are no longer afraid. With this justification we can answer all the roaring and railing of Satan and of ungodly people. With this we shall be able to die; with this we shall rise again boldly and face the last great court of judgment.

Bold shall I stand in that great day,
For who aught to my charge shall lay?
While by my Lord absolved I am
From sin's tremendous curse and blame.

Friend, the Lord can blot out all your sins. I am not taking a shot in the dark when I say this. “All manner of sin and of blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men.” Though you are steeped in crime up to your throat, He can remove the defilement with a word and say, “I will, be thou clean.” The Lord is a great forgiver.

“I believe in the Forgiveness of Sins.” Do you?

Even at this hour He can pronounce the sentence, “Thy sins be forgiven thee; go in peace”; and if He does, no power in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, can put you under suspicion, let alone under wrath. Do not doubt the power of almighty love. You could not forgive your fellow man if he had offended you as you have offended God; but you must not measure God’s corn with your own bushel. His thoughts and ways are as far above yours as the heavens are high above the earth.

“Well,” you say, “it would be a great miracle if the Lord were to pardon me.” Exactly. It would be a supreme miracle — and that is why He is likely to do it; for He does “great things and unsearchable” which we never expected.

I myself was struck down with a horrible sense of guilt that made my life a misery. But when I heard the command, “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is none else” — I looked, and in a moment the Lord justified me. What I saw was Jesus Christ, made sin for me, and that sight gave me rest. When those who had been bitten by the fiery serpents in the wilderness looked at the bronze serpent, they were healed at once; and so was I when I looked to the crucified Saviour. The Holy Spirit, who enabled me to believe, gave me peace through believing. I felt as sure that I was forgiven as I had felt sure before that I was condemned. I had been certain of my condemnation because the Word of God declared it and my conscience bore witness to it; but when the Lord justified me, the same witnesses made me equally certain of that. The word of the Lord in the Scripture says, “He that believeth on him is not condemned,” and my conscience bears witness that I believed, and that God is just in pardoning me. So I have the witness of the Holy Spirit and of my own conscience, and these two agree as one. Oh, how I wish my reader would accept God’s testimony on this matter! Then very soon he would have the witness in himself as well.

I dare to say that a sinner justified by God stands on even firmer ground than a righteous man justified by his works — if there were such a man. We could never be sure we had done enough works. Our conscience would always be uneasy in case we fell short after all, and we would have nothing to rely on but the trembling verdict of a judgment that can be wrong. But when God Himself justifies, and the Holy Spirit bears witness to it by giving us peace with God, then we feel that the matter is sure and settled, and we enter into rest. No tongue can describe the depth of the calm that comes over the soul that has received the peace of God which passeth all understanding.

fields.title: Just and the Justifier
fields.body_html:
WE HAVE SEEN the ungodly justified, and we have considered the great truth that only God can justify anyone. Now we go a step further and ask: How can a just God justify guilty people? Here we find a full answer in the words of Paul in Romans 3:21-26. We will read six verses from the chapter so as to follow the flow of the passage:

“But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference; for all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; to declare, I say, at this time his righteousness; that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.”

Let me share a bit of personal experience here. When I was under the hand of the Holy Spirit, under conviction of sin, I had a clear and sharp sense of God’s justice. Whatever sin might be to other people, to me it became an unbearable burden. It was not so much that I feared hell; I feared sin. I knew I was so horribly guilty that I remember feeling that if God did not punish me for sin, He ought to. I felt that the Judge of all the earth ought to condemn sin like mine. I sat on the judgment seat and sentenced myself to perish; for I admitted that if I had been God, I could have done nothing else but send a guilty creature like me down to the lowest hell. All the while, my mind was deeply concerned for the honour of God’s name and the integrity of His moral government. I felt that my conscience would not be satisfied if I could be forgiven unjustly. fields.title: Concerning Deliverance from Sinning
fields.body_html:
AT THIS POINT I want to say a plain word or two to those who understand the way of justification by faith which is in Christ Jesus, but whose trouble is that they cannot stop sinning. We can never be happy, at rest, or spiritually healthy until we become holy. We must be rid of sin; but how is that to be done? For many people this is the question of life or death. The old nature is very strong. They have tried to curb it and tame it, but it will not be subdued; and though they long to be better, they find themselves, if anything, growing worse than before. The heart is so hard, the will so stubborn, the passions so furious, the thoughts so restless, the imagination so unruly, the desires so wild, that a person feels he has a den of wild beasts inside him that would sooner eat him up than be ruled by him. We may say of our fallen nature what the Lord said to Job about Leviathan: “Wilt thou play with him as with a bird? or wilt thou bind him for thy maidens?” A man might as well hope to hold the north wind in the hollow of his hand as expect to control, by his own strength, the turbulent powers that live in his fallen nature. This is a greater feat than any of the legendary labours of Hercules: God is needed here.

“I could believe that Jesus would forgive sin,” someone says, “but my trouble is that I sin again, and I feel such terrible tendencies to evil inside me. Just as surely as a stone thrown up into the air soon falls back to the ground, so I — though earnest preaching sends me up towards heaven — soon fall back into my old numbness. Sadly, I am easily mesmerised by the deadly eyes of sin, and held as if under a spell, so that I cannot escape from my own folly.”

Dear friend, salvation would be a sadly incomplete affair if it did not deal with this part of our ruined condition. We need to be purified as well as pardoned. Justification without sanctification would not be salvation at all. It would pronounce the leper clean and leave him to die of his disease; it would forgive the rebellion and let the rebel remain his king’s enemy. It would remove the consequences but ignore the cause, and that would leave us an endless and hopeless task. It would stop the stream for a while, but leave an open fountain of defilement that would sooner or later burst out with greater force. Remember that the Lord Jesus came to take away sin in three ways: He came to remove the penalty of sin, the power of sin, and finally the presence of sin. You may reach the second part at once — the power of sin can be broken immediately — and so you will be on the road to the third, the removal of sin’s very presence. “We know that he was manifested to take away our sins.”

The angel said of our Lord, “Thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins.” Our Lord Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil in us. What was said at our Lord’s birth was declared again at His death; for when the soldier pierced His side, forthwith came there out blood and water, to show the double cure by which we are set free from both the guilt and the defilement of sin.

But if you are troubled about the power of sin and the tendencies of your nature — as well you may be — here is a promise for you. Have faith in it, for it stands in that covenant of grace which is ordered in all things and sure. God, who cannot lie, has said in Ezekiel 36:26:

“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.”

You see, it is all “I will” and “I will.” “I will give” and “I will take away.” This is the royal language of the King of kings, who is able to accomplish everything He wills. Not one of His words will ever fall to the ground.

The Lord knows perfectly well that you cannot change your own heart or cleanse your own nature; but He also knows that He can do both. He can make the Ethiopian change his skin and the leopard his spots. Listen to this and be astonished: He can create you a second time; He can cause you to be born again. This is a miracle of grace, but the Holy Ghost will perform it. It would be an extraordinary thing if someone could stand at the foot of Niagara Falls and speak a word that made the Niagara River start running upstream and leap up that great cliff over which it now pours with tremendous force. Nothing but the power of God could achieve that marvel; yet it would be no more than a fitting comparison for what would happen if the course of your nature were completely reversed. All things are possible with God. He can reverse the direction of your desires and the current of your life, and instead of your whole being flowing downward away from God, He can make it tend upward toward God. In fact, that is what the Lord has promised to do for all who are in the covenant; and we know from Scripture that all believers are in the covenant. Let me read the words again:

“A new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give an heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 11:19).

What a wonderful promise! And it is yea and amen in Christ Jesus to the glory of God by us. Let us take hold of it, accept it as true, and claim it for ourselves. Then it will be fulfilled in us, and in the days and years to come we will be singing of the wonderful change that God’s sovereign grace has worked in us.

It is well worth noticing that when the Lord takes away the stony heart, the deed is done. And once it is done, no known power can ever take away the new heart He gives and the right spirit He puts within us. “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” — that is, without repentance on His part; He does not take back what He has once given. Let Him renew you, and you will be renewed. Human reforms and clean-ups soon come to an end, for the dog returns to his vomit; but when God puts a new heart into us, the new heart is there for ever, and it will never harden into stone again. He who made it flesh will keep it so. In this we may rejoice and be glad for ever — in what God creates in the kingdom of His grace.

To put it very simply — have you ever heard Mr. Rowland Hill’s illustration of the cat and the sow? I will tell it my own way, to illustrate our Saviour’s vivid words, “Ye must be born again.” Do you see that cat? What a clean creature she is! How cleverly she washes herself with her tongue and her paws! It is really a pretty sight! Have you ever seen a sow do that? No, you never have. It is against its nature. It would rather wallow in the mud. Go and teach a sow to wash itself, and see how little success you have. It would be a great improvement in hygiene if pigs would keep clean. Teach them to wash and clean themselves the way the cat has been doing! It is a useless task. You may wash that sow by force, but it hurries back to the mud and is soon as filthy as ever. The only way to get a sow to wash itself is to turn it into a cat. Then it will wash and be clean — but not until then! Suppose that transformation were accomplished: what was difficult or impossible becomes easy enough, and from then on the pig would be fit for your sitting room and your hearth-rug. It is the same with an ungodly man. You cannot force him to do what a renewed man does most willingly. You may teach him and set him a good example, but he cannot learn the art of holiness, because he has no heart for it; his nature leads him another way. When the Lord makes a new man of him, everything looks different. The change is so great that I once heard a convert say, “Either the whole world has changed, or else I have.” The new nature pursues what is right as naturally as the old nature wanders after what is wrong. What a blessing to receive such a nature! Only the Holy Ghost can give it.

Has it ever struck you what a wonderful thing it is for the Lord to give someone a new heart and a right spirit? Perhaps you have seen a lobster that has fought with another lobster and lost one of its claws, and a new claw has grown. That is a remarkable thing; but it is far more astounding that a man should be given a new heart. This truly is a miracle beyond the powers of nature. Here is a tree. If you cut off one of its branches, another may grow in its place; but can you change the tree? Can you sweeten sour sap? Can you make the thorn bear figs? You can graft something better into it, and that is the picture nature gives us of the work of grace; but to change the very life-sap of the tree completely would be a miracle indeed. That is the kind of wonder and mystery of power that God works in all who believe in Jesus.

If you give yourself up to His divine working, the Lord will change your nature. He will subdue the old nature and breathe new life into you. Put your trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, and He will take the stony heart out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. Where everything was hard, everything will be tender; where everything was vicious, everything will be virtuous; where everything tended downward, everything will rise upward with eager force. The lion of anger will give way to the lamb of meekness; the raven of uncleanness will fly away before the dove of purity; the vile serpent of deceit will be trampled under the heel of truth.

I have seen with my own eyes such marvellous changes in moral and spiritual character that I despair of no one. If it were appropriate, I could point out women who were once immoral and are now as pure as freshly fallen snow, and men who used to blaspheme who now delight everyone around them with their intense devotion. Thieves are made honest, drunkards sober, liars truthful, and scoffers zealous. Wherever the grace of God has appeared to a man, it has trained him to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present evil world; and, dear reader, it will do the same for you.

“I can’t make this change,” someone says. Who said you could? The Scripture we have quoted speaks not of what man will do, but of what God will do. It is God’s promise, and it is up to Him to keep His own commitments. Trust Him to keep His Word to you, and it will be done.

“But how is it to be done?” What business is that of yours? Must the Lord explain His methods before you will believe Him? The Lord’s working in this matter is a great mystery: the Holy Ghost performs it. The One who made the promise is responsible for keeping it, and He is equal to the task. God, who promises this marvellous change, will certainly carry it out in all who receive Jesus, for to all such He gives power to become the sons of God. Oh, that you would believe it! Oh, that you would do the gracious Lord the justice of believing that He can and will do this for you, great miracle though it will be! Oh, that you would believe that God cannot lie! Oh, that you would trust Him for a new heart and a right spirit, for He can give them to you! May the Lord give you faith in His promise, faith in His Son, faith in the Holy Spirit, and faith in Him; and to Him be praise and honour and glory for ever and ever! Amen.

God, who cannot lie, has said in Ezekiel 36:26: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” You see, it is all “I will” and “I will.” “I will give” and “I will take away.” This is the royal language of the King of kings, who is able to accomplish everything He wills. Not one of His words will ever fall to the ground. The Lord knows perfectly well that you cannot change your own heart or cleanse your own nature; but He also knows that He can do both. He can make the Ethiopian change his skin and the leopard his spots. Listen to this and be astonished: He can create you a second time; He can cause you to be born again. This is a miracle of grace, but the Holy Ghost will perform it. It would be an extraordinary thing if someone could stand at the foot of Niagara Falls and speak a word that made the Niagara River start running upstream and leap up that great cliff over which it now pours with tremendous force. Nothing but the power of God could achieve that marvel; yet it would be no more than a fitting comparison for what would happen if the course of your nature were completely reversed. All things are possible with God. He can reverse the direction of your desires and the current of your life, and instead of your whole being flowing downward away from God, He can make it tend upward toward God. In fact, that is what the Lord has promised to do for all who are in the covenant; and we know from Scripture that all believers are in the covenant. Let me read the words again: “A new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give an heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 11:19). What a wonderful promise! And it is yea and amen in Christ Jesus to the glory of God by us. Let us take hold of it, accept it as true, and claim it for ourselves. Then it will be fulfilled in us, and in the days and years to come we will be singing of the wonderful change that God’s sovereign grace has worked in us. It is well worth noticing that when the Lord takes away the stony heart, the deed is done. And once it is done, no known power can ever take away the new heart He gives and the right spirit He puts within us. “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” — that is, without repentance on His part; He does not take back what He has once given. Let Him renew you, and you will be renewed. Human reforms and clean-ups soon come to an end, for the dog returns to his vomit; but when God puts a new heart into us, the new heart is there for ever, and it will never harden into stone again. He who made it flesh will keep it so. In this we may rejoice and be glad for ever — in what God creates in the kingdom of His grace. To put it very simply — have you ever heard Mr. Rowland Hill’s illustration of the cat and the sow? I will tell it my own way, to illustrate our Saviour’s vivid words, “Ye must be born again.” Do you see that cat? What a clean creature she is! How cleverly she washes herself with her tongue and her paws! It is really a pretty sight! Have you ever seen a sow do that? No, you never have. It is against its nature. It would rather wallow in the mud. Go and teach a sow to wash itself, and see how little success you have. It would be a great improvement in hygiene if pigs would keep clean. Teach them to wash and clean themselves the way the cat has been doing! It is a useless task. You may wash that sow by force, but it hurries back to the mud and is soon as filthy as ever. The only way to get a sow to wash itself is to turn it into a cat. Then it will wash and be clean — but not until then! Suppose that transformation were accomplished: what was difficult or impossible becomes easy enough, and from then on the pig would be fit for your sitting room and your hearth-rug. It is the same with an ungodly man. You cannot force him to do what a renewed man does most willingly. You may teach him and set him a good example, but he cannot learn the art of holiness, because he has no heart for it; his nature leads him another way. When the Lord makes a new man of him, everything looks different. The change is so great that I once heard a convert say, “Either the whole world has changed, or else I have.” The new nature pursues what is right as naturally as the old nature wanders after what is wrong. What a blessing to receive such a nature! Only the Holy Ghost can give it. Has it ever struck you what a wonderful thing it is for the Lord to give someone a new heart and a right spirit? Perhaps you have seen a lobster that has fought with another lobster and lost one of its claws, and a new claw has grown. That is a remarkable thing; but it is far more astounding that a man should be given a new heart. This truly is a miracle beyond the powers of nature. Here is a tree. If you cut off one of its branches, another may grow in its place; but can you change the tree? Can you sweeten sour sap? Can you make the thorn bear figs? You can graft something better into it, and that is the picture nature gives us of the work of grace; but to change the very life-sap of the tree completely would be a miracle indeed. That is the kind of wonder and mystery of power that God works in all who believe in Jesus. If you give yourself up to His divine working, the Lord will change your nature. He will subdue the old nature and breathe new life into you. Put your trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, and He will take the stony heart out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. Where everything was hard, everything will be tender; where everything was vicious, everything will be virtuous; where everything tended downward, everything will rise upward with eager force. The lion of anger will give way to the lamb of meekness; the raven of uncleanness will fly away before the dove of purity; the vile serpent of deceit will be trampled under the heel of truth. I have seen with my own eyes such marvellous changes in moral and spiritual character that I despair of no one. If it were appropriate, I could point out women who were once immoral and are now as pure as freshly fallen snow, and men who used to blaspheme who now delight everyone around them with their intense devotion. Thieves are made honest, drunkards sober, liars truthful, and scoffers zealous. Wherever the grace of God has appeared to a man, it has trained him to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present evil world; and, dear reader, it will do the same for you. “I can’t make this change,” someone says. Who said you could? The Scripture we have quoted speaks not of what man will do, but of what God will do. It is God’s promise, and it is up to Him to keep His own commitments. Trust Him to keep His Word to you, and it will be done. “But how is it to be done?” What business is that of yours? Must the Lord explain His methods before you will believe Him? The Lord’s working in this matter is a great mystery: the Holy Ghost performs it. The One who made the promise is responsible for keeping it, and He is equal to the task. God, who promises this marvellous change, will certainly carry it out in all who receive Jesus, for to all such He gives power to become the sons of God. Oh, that you would believe it! Oh, that you would do the gracious Lord the justice of believing that He can and will do this for you, great miracle though it will be! Oh, that you would believe that God cannot lie! Oh, that you would trust Him for a new heart and a right spirit, for He can give them to you! May the Lord give you faith in His promise, faith in His Son, faith in the Holy Spirit, and faith in Him; and to Him be praise and honour and glory for ever and ever! Amen.

fields.title: By Grace Through Faith
fields.body_html:
“By grace are ye saved, through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).

I THINK IT WORTHWHILE to step aside for a moment and ask my reader to look, with adoration, at the fountain-head of our salvation, which is the grace of God. “By grace are ye saved.” It is because God is gracious that sinful people are forgiven, converted, purified and saved. They are not saved because of anything in them, or anything that ever could be in them, but because of the boundless love, goodness, pity, compassion, mercy and grace of God. So linger a moment at the spring. See the pure river of water of life as it flows out of the throne of God and of the Lamb!

What a bottomless ocean the grace of God is! Who can measure its breadth? Who can sound its depth? Like all God’s other attributes, it is infinite. God is full of love, for “God is love.” God is full of goodness; the very name “God” is short for “good.” Unlimited goodness and love are part of the very essence of the Godhead. It is because “his mercy endureth for ever” that people are not destroyed; because “his compassions fail not” that sinners are brought to Him and forgiven.

Remember this; otherwise you may fall into error by fixing your mind so firmly on faith, which is the channel of salvation, that you forget grace, which is the fountain and source of faith itself. Faith is the work of God’s grace in us. No man can say that Jesus is the Christ but by the Holy Ghost. “No man cometh unto me,” saith Jesus, “except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” So faith, which is coming to Christ, is the result of God drawing us. Grace is the first and last moving cause of salvation; and faith, essential as it is, is only one important part of the machinery that grace uses. We are saved “through faith,” but salvation is “by grace.” Sound out those words as if with the archangel’s trumpet: “By grace are ye saved.” What good news for the undeserving!

Faith acts as a channel or pipe. Grace is the fountain and the stream; faith is the aqueduct along which the flood of mercy flows down to refresh thirsty people. It is a great pity when the aqueduct is broken. Around Rome it is a sad sight to see the many noble aqueducts that no longer carry water into the city, because the arches are broken and those marvellous structures lie in ruins. The aqueduct must be kept whole to carry the current; and in the same way, faith must be true and sound, reaching right up to God and coming right down to us, if it is to be a useful channel of mercy to our souls.

Still, I remind you again that faith is only the channel or aqueduct, not the fountain-head, and we must not look at it so much that we exalt it above the divine source of every blessing, which is the grace of God. Never make a Christ out of your faith, or think of it as if it were the independent source of your salvation. Our life is found in “looking unto Jesus,” not in looking at our own faith. By faith all things become possible to us; yet the power is not in the faith, but in the God on whom faith relies. Grace is the mighty engine, and faith is the coupling by which the carriage of the soul is attached to that great driving power. The righteousness of faith is not the moral excellence of faith, but the righteousness of Jesus Christ, which faith grasps and makes its own. The peace in the soul does not come from contemplating our own faith. It comes to us from Him who is our peace: faith touches the hem of His garment, and power flows out of Him into the soul.

So you see, dear friend, the weakness of your faith will not destroy you. A trembling hand can receive a golden gift. The Lord’s salvation can come to us even if our faith is only as a grain of mustard seed. The power lies in the grace of God, not in our faith. Great messages can be sent along thin wires, and the peace-giving witness of the Holy Spirit can reach the heart through a thread-like faith that seems hardly able to bear its own weight. Think more about Him you are looking to than about the look itself. You must look away even from your own looking, and see nothing but Jesus, and the grace of God revealed in Him.

fields.title: Faith, What Is It?
fields.body_html:
WHAT IS THIS FAITH of which it is said, “By grace are ye saved, through faith”? There are many descriptions of faith; but almost every definition I have come across has left me understanding it less than I did before I read it. There is an old story of a man who said, before reading the chapter aloud, that he would “confound” it; and very likely he did, though he meant to “expound” it. We can explain faith until nobody understands it. I hope I will not be guilty of that. Faith is the simplest of all things, and perhaps because it is so simple, it is all the harder to explain.

What is faith? It is made up of three things: knowledge, belief and trust. Knowledge comes first. “How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?” I need to be told a fact before I can possibly believe it. “Faith cometh by hearing”; we must first hear, so that we may know what is to be believed. “They that know thy name shall put their trust in thee.” A measure of knowledge is essential to faith; that is why it matters so much to gain knowledge. “Incline your ear, and come unto me; hear, and your soul shall live.” That was the word of the ancient prophet, and it is still the word of the gospel. Search the Scriptures and learn what the Holy Spirit teaches about Christ and His salvation. Seek to know God: “For he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.” May the Holy Spirit give you the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord! Know the gospel: know what the good news is — how it speaks of free forgiveness, of a change of heart, of adoption into the family of God, and of countless other blessings. Above all, know Christ Jesus, the Son of God, the Saviour of men — united to us by His human nature, and yet one with God. So He is able to act as Mediator between God and man, to lay His hand on both, and to be the connecting link between the sinner and the Judge of all the earth. Try to know more and more of Christ Jesus. Try especially to know the doctrine of Christ’s sacrifice; for the point on which saving faith chiefly fastens is this: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them.” Know that Jesus was “made a curse for us, as it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” Drink deeply of the doctrine of Christ’s substitutionary work; for in it lies the sweetest possible comfort for guilty people, since the Lord “made him to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” Faith begins with knowledge.

Next, the mind goes on to believe that these things are true. The soul believes that God exists and that He hears the cries of sincere hearts; that the gospel comes from God; that justification by faith is the grand truth God has revealed by His Spirit in these last days more clearly than before. Then the heart believes that Jesus is truly and really our God and Saviour, the Redeemer of men, the Prophet, Priest and King of His people. All this is accepted as certain truth, not to be questioned. I pray that you may come to this at once. Come to believe firmly that “the blood of Jesus Christ, God’s dear Son, cleanseth us from all sin”; that His sacrifice is complete and fully accepted by God on our behalf, so that whoever believes in Jesus is not condemned. Believe these truths just as you believe any other statements; for the difference between ordinary faith and saving faith lies mainly in what it is exercised on. Believe the witness of God just as you believe the word of your own father or friend. “If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater.”

So far you have moved toward faith; only one more ingredient is needed to complete it, and that is trust. Commit yourself to the merciful God; rest your hope on the gracious gospel; trust your soul to the Saviour who died and lives; wash away your sins in the atoning blood; accept His perfect righteousness, and all is well. Trust is the lifeblood of faith; there is no saving faith without it. The Puritans used to explain faith by the word “recumbency.” It meant leaning on something. Lean your whole weight on Christ. A better picture still would be to say: fall full length and lie on the Rock of Ages. Throw yourself on Jesus; rest in Him; commit yourself to Him. Once you have done that, you have exercised saving faith. Faith is not a blind thing, for faith begins with knowledge. It is not a theoretical thing, for faith believes facts it is sure of. It is not an impractical, dreamy thing, for faith trusts, and stakes its destiny on the truth of revelation. That is one way of describing what faith is.

Let me try again. Faith is believing that Christ is what He is said to be, and that He will do what He has promised to do — and then expecting this from Him. The Scriptures speak of Jesus Christ as God in human flesh; as perfect in His character; as made a sin-offering on our behalf; as bearing our sins in His own body on the tree. Scripture speaks of Him as having finished transgression, made an end of sin, and brought in everlasting righteousness. The sacred records tell us further that He “rose again from the dead,” that He “ever liveth to make intercession for us,” that He has gone up into glory and taken possession of heaven on behalf of His people, and that He will soon come again “to judge the world in righteousness, and his people with equity.” We are to believe most firmly that this is so; for this is the testimony of God the Father when He said, “This is my beloved Son; hear ye him.” God the Holy Spirit testifies to it too; for the Spirit has borne witness to Christ in the inspired Word, through various miracles, and by His working in people’s hearts. We are to believe that this testimony is true.

Faith also believes that Christ will do what He has promised. Since He has promised to cast out none who come to Him, it is certain He will not cast us out if we come to Him. Faith believes that since Jesus said, “The water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life,” it must be true; and if we receive this living water from Christ, it will remain in us and well up within us in streams of holy life. Whatever Christ has promised to do, He will do; and we must believe this, and so look to His hands for pardon, justification, preservation and eternal glory, just as He has promised them to those who believe in Him.

Then comes the next necessary step. Jesus is what He is said to be; Jesus will do what He says He will do; so each of us must trust Him, saying, “He will be to me what He says He is, and He will do for me what He has promised to do. I leave myself in the hands of the One appointed to save, so that He may save me. I rest on His promise that He will do just as He has said.” This is saving faith, and he that hath it hath everlasting life. Whatever his dangers and difficulties, whatever his darkness and depression, whatever his weaknesses and sins, the one who believes in Christ Jesus in this way is not condemned, and will never come into condemnation.

May that explanation be of some help! I trust the Spirit of God may use it to lead my reader into peace right away. “Be not afraid; only believe.” Trust, and be at rest.

My fear is that the reader may be content with understanding what needs to be done, and yet never do it. The poorest real faith actually at work is better than the finest ideal of faith left in the realm of theory. The great thing is to believe in the Lord Jesus at once. Never mind distinctions and definitions. A hungry man eats even though he does not understand what his food is made of, how his mouth is put together, or how digestion works: he lives because he eats. Another, far cleverer person understands the science of nutrition thoroughly; but if he does not eat, he will die, knowledge and all. No doubt there are many in hell at this hour who understood the doctrine of faith but did not believe. On the other hand, not one person who has trusted in the Lord Jesus has ever been cast out, though he may never have been able to define his faith intelligently. Oh, dear reader, receive the Lord Jesus into your soul, and you will live for ever! “He that believeth in Him hath everlasting life.”

fields.title: How May Faith Be Illustrated?
fields.body_html:
TO MAKE THE MATTER of faith clearer still, I will give you a few illustrations. Though only the Holy Spirit can make my reader see, it is my duty and my joy to give all the light I can, and to pray the divine Lord to open blind eyes. Oh, that my reader would pray the same prayer for himself!

The faith which saves has its analogies in the human frame.
It is the eye which looks. By the eye we bring into the mind that which is far away; we can bring the sun and the far-off stars into the mind by a glance of the eye. So by trust we bring the Lord Jesus near to us; and though He be far away in Heaven, He enters into our heart. Only look to Jesus; for the hymn is strictly true—
There is life in a look at the Crucified One,

fields.title: Why Are We Saved by Faith?
fields.body_html:
WHY HAS FAITH BEEN CHOSEN as the channel of salvation? No doubt people often ask this. “By grace are ye saved through faith” is certainly the teaching of Holy Scripture and the appointment of God; but why is it so? Why was faith chosen rather than hope, or love, or patience?

We ought to be modest in answering such a question, for God’s ways cannot always be understood, and we are not allowed to question them presumptuously. We would humbly answer that, as far as we can tell, faith has been chosen as the channel of grace because faith is naturally suited to be the receiver. Suppose I am about to give a poor man a gift of money. I put it into his hand — why? Well, it would hardly be fitting to put it in his ear or lay it on his foot; the hand seems made on purpose to receive. In the same way, in the make-up of our minds, faith is created on purpose to be a receiver. It is a person’s hand, and there is a fitness in receiving grace by means of it.

Let me put this very plainly. The faith that receives Christ is as simple an act as your child taking an apple from you, because you hold it out and promise to give it to him if he comes for it. That believing and receiving concern only an apple; but they make up exactly the same act as the faith that deals with eternal salvation. What the child’s hand is to the apple, your faith is to Christ’s perfect salvation. The child’s hand does not make the apple, or improve the apple, or earn the apple; it only takes it. And God has chosen faith to be the receiver of salvation because it does not pretend to create salvation or to help with it, but is content to receive it humbly. “Faith is the tongue that begs pardon, the hand that receives it, and the eye that sees it; but it is not the price that buys it.” Faith never makes herself her own plea; she rests her whole case on the blood of Christ. She makes a good servant for bringing the riches of the Lord Jesus to the soul, because she acknowledges where she got them from, and admits that grace alone entrusted her with them.

Again, faith has no doubt been chosen because it gives all the glory to God. It is of faith that it might be by grace, and it is of grace so that there might be no boasting; for God cannot bear pride. “The proud he knoweth afar off,” and He has no wish to come any nearer to them. He will not give salvation in a way that would suggest or encourage pride. Paul says, “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” Now, faith shuts out all boasting. The hand that receives charity does not say, “I should be thanked for accepting the gift”; that would be absurd. When the hand carries bread to the mouth, it does not say to the body, “Thank me, because I feed you.” What the hand does is a very simple thing, though a very necessary one; and it never claims any glory for what it does. So God has chosen faith to receive the indescribable gift of His grace, because faith cannot take any credit for itself, but must adore the gracious God who is the giver of every good thing. Faith puts the crown on the right head; and that is why the Lord Jesus used to put the crown on the head of faith, saying, “Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.”

Next, God chooses faith as the channel of salvation because it is a sure way of linking a person with God. When someone trusts in God, there is a point of union between them, and that union guarantees blessing. Faith saves us because it makes us cling to God, and so brings us into connection with Him. I have often used the following illustration, but I must repeat it, because I cannot think of a better one. I am told that years ago a boat overturned above Niagara Falls, and two men were being swept down by the current. People on the bank managed to float a rope out to them, and both men seized it. One of them held on tight and was pulled safely to the bank. But the other, seeing a great log come floating by, foolishly let go of the rope and clung to the log, because it was the bigger of the two and seemed better to hold on to. Alas! The log, with the man on it, went right over into the vast abyss, because there was no connection between the log and the shore. The size of the log did him no good; what was needed for safety was a connection with the shore. In the same way, when a person trusts in his works, or in sacraments, or in anything of that kind, he will not be saved, because there is no link between him and Christ. But faith, though it may seem like a slender cord, is held at the shore end by the great God. Infinite power pulls in the connecting line, and so draws the person away from destruction. Oh, the blessedness of faith, because it unites us to God!

Faith is chosen, again, because it touches the springs of action. Even in ordinary things, faith of some kind lies at the root of everything. I wonder if I would be wrong to say that we never do anything except through faith of one sort or another. If I walk across my study, it is because I believe my legs will carry me. A man eats because he believes he needs food; he goes to work because he believes in the value of money; he accepts a cheque because he believes the bank will honour it. Columbus discovered America because he believed there was another continent beyond the ocean; and the Pilgrim Fathers settled there because they believed God would be with them on those rocky shores. Most great deeds have been born of faith. For good or for evil, faith works wonders through the person in whom it lives. In its natural form, faith is an all-powerful force that enters into every kind of human action. Very possibly the man who mocks faith in God is the one who has the most faith of an evil kind; in fact, he usually falls into a gullibility that would be ridiculous if it were not disgraceful. God gives salvation to faith because, by creating faith in us, He touches the real mainspring of our emotions and actions. He has, so to speak, taken possession of the battery, and now He can send the sacred current to every part of our nature. When we believe in Christ, and the heart has come into God’s possession, then we are saved from sin and moved toward repentance, holiness, zeal, prayer, consecration, and every other gracious thing. “What oil is to the wheels, what weights are to a clock, what wings are to a bird, what sails are to a ship, that faith is to all holy duties and services.” Have faith, and all the other graces will follow and keep on their course.

Faith, again, has the power of working by love. It moves the affections toward God and draws the heart after the best things. Whoever believes in God will, beyond all question, love God. Faith is an act of the understanding, but it also comes from the heart. “With the heart man believeth unto righteousness.” So God gives salvation to faith because faith lives next door to the affections and is a close relative of love; and love is the parent and nurse of every holy feeling and act. Love to God is obedience; love to God is holiness. To love God and to love our neighbour is to be conformed to the image of Christ; and this is salvation.

Moreover, faith creates peace and joy. The one who has it is at rest; he is calm, glad and joyful; and this is a preparation for heaven. God gives all heavenly gifts to faith for this reason, among others: faith works in us the life and spirit that are to be displayed for ever in the higher and better world. Faith gives us armour for this life and education for the life to come. It enables a person both to live and to die without fear; it prepares us both for action and for suffering. That is why the Lord chooses it as a most suitable means of conveying grace to us, and so making us sure of glory.

Certainly faith does for us what nothing else can do: it gives us joy and peace and brings us into rest. Why do people try to gain salvation by other means? An old preacher says, “A foolish servant who is told to open a door puts his shoulder to it and pushes with all his might; but the door does not budge, and however much strength he uses, he cannot get in. Another comes with a key, unlocks the door easily, and walks straight in. Those who would be saved by works are pushing at heaven’s gate with no result; but faith is the key that opens the gate at once.” Reader, won’t you use that key? The Lord commands you to believe in His dear Son, so you may do so; and if you do, you will live. Is not this the promise of the gospel: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved”? (Mark 16:16). What objection can you have to a way of salvation that so clearly shows the mercy and the wisdom of our gracious God?
