When the hand carries bread to the mouth, it does not say to the body, “Thank me, because I feed you.” What the hand does is a very simple thing, though a very necessary one; and it never claims any glory for what it does. So God has chosen faith to receive the indescribable gift of His grace, because faith cannot take any credit for itself, but must adore the gracious God who is the giver of every good thing. Faith puts the crown on the right head; and that is why the Lord Jesus used to put the crown on the head of faith, saying, “Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” Next, God chooses faith as the channel of salvation because it is a sure way of linking a person with God. When someone trusts in God, there is a point of union between them, and that union guarantees blessing. Faith saves us because it makes us cling to God, and so brings us into connection with Him. I have often used the following illustration, but I must repeat it, because I cannot think of a better one. I am told that years ago a boat overturned above Niagara Falls, and two men were being swept down by the current. People on the bank managed to float a rope out to them, and both men seized it. One of them held on tight and was pulled safely to the bank. But the other, seeing a great log come floating by, foolishly let go of the rope and clung to the log, because it was the bigger of the two and seemed better to hold on to. Alas! The log, with the man on it, went right over into the vast abyss, because there was no connection between the log and the shore. The size of the log did him no good; what was needed for safety was a connection with the shore. In the same way, when a person trusts in his works, or in sacraments, or in anything of that kind, he will not be saved, because there is no link between him and Christ. But faith, though it may seem like a slender cord, is held at the shore end by the great God. Infinite power pulls in the connecting line, and so draws the person away from destruction. Oh, the blessedness of faith, because it unites us to God! Faith is chosen, again, because it touches the springs of action. Even in ordinary things, faith of some kind lies at the root of everything. I wonder if I would be wrong to say that we never do anything except through faith of one sort or another. If I walk across my study, it is because I believe my legs will carry me. A man eats because he believes he needs food; he goes to work because he believes in the value of money; he accepts a cheque because he believes the bank will honour it. Columbus discovered America because he believed there was another continent beyond the ocean; and the Pilgrim Fathers settled there because they believed God would be with them on those rocky shores. Most great deeds have been born of faith. For good or for evil, faith works wonders through the person in whom it lives. In its natural form, faith is an all-powerful force that enters into every kind of human action. Very possibly the man who mocks faith in God is the one who has the most faith of an evil kind; in fact, he usually falls into a gullibility that would be ridiculous if it were not disgraceful. God gives salvation to faith because, by creating faith in us, He touches the real mainspring of our emotions and actions. He has, so to speak, taken possession of the battery, and now He can send the sacred current to every part of our nature. When we believe in Christ, and the heart has come into God’s possession, then we are saved from sin and moved toward repentance, holiness, zeal, prayer, consecration, and every other gracious thing. “What oil is to the wheels, what weights are to a clock, what wings are to a bird, what sails are to a ship, that faith is to all holy duties and services.” Have faith, and all the other graces will follow and keep on their course. Faith, again, has the power of working by love. It moves the affections toward God and draws the heart after the best things. Whoever believes in God will, beyond all question, love God. Faith is an act of the understanding, but it also comes from the heart. “With the heart man believeth unto righteousness.” So God gives salvation to faith because faith lives next door to the affections and is a close relative of love; and love is the parent and nurse of every holy feeling and act. Love to God is obedience; love to God is holiness. To love God and to love our neighbour is to be conformed to the image of Christ; and this is salvation. Moreover, faith creates peace and joy. The one who has it is at rest; he is calm, glad and joyful; and this is a preparation for heaven. God gives all heavenly gifts to faith for this reason, among others: faith works in us the life and spirit that are to be displayed for ever in the higher and better world. Faith gives us armour for this life and education for the life to come. It enables a person both to live and to die without fear; it prepares us both for action and for suffering. That is why the Lord chooses it as a most suitable means of conveying grace to us, and so making us sure of glory. Certainly faith does for us what nothing else can do: it gives us joy and peace and brings us into rest. Why do people try to gain salvation by other means? An old preacher says, “A foolish servant who is told to open a door puts his shoulder to it and pushes with all his might; but the door does not budge, and however much strength he uses, he cannot get in. Another comes with a key, unlocks the door easily, and walks straight in. Those who would be saved by works are pushing at heaven’s gate with no result; but faith is the key that opens the gate at once.” Reader, won’t you use that key? The Lord commands you to believe in His dear Son, so you may do so; and if you do, you will live. Is not this the promise of the gospel: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved”? (Mark 16:16). What objection can you have to a way of salvation that so clearly shows the mercy and the wisdom of our gracious God?

fields.title: Alas! I Can Do Nothing!
fields.body_html:
ONCE THE ANXIOUS HEART has accepted the doctrine of the atonement, and learned the great truth that salvation is by faith in the Lord Jesus, it is often deeply troubled by a sense of being unable to do anything good. Many people are groaning, “I can do nothing.” They are not turning this into an excuse; they feel it as a daily burden. They would if they could. Each of them can honestly say, “To will is present with me, but how to perform that which I would I find not.”

This feeling seems to make the whole gospel null and void; for what use is food to a hungry man if he cannot get at it? What good is the river of the water of life if you cannot drink? We remember the story of the doctor and the poor woman’s child. The wise physician told the mother that her little one would soon be better with proper treatment, but that it was absolutely necessary for her boy to drink the best wine regularly and to spend some time at one of the German spas. This, to a widow who could hardly get bread to eat! Now, it sometimes seems to the troubled heart that the simple gospel of “Believe and live” is not so very simple after all, because it asks the poor sinner to do what he cannot do. To someone who is truly awakened but only half taught, there seems to be a missing link. There is the salvation of Jesus — but how is it to be reached? The soul has no strength and does not know what to do. It lies within sight of the city of refuge and cannot get through its gate.

Has the plan of salvation made provision for this lack of strength? It has. The Lord’s work is perfect. It begins where we are, and asks nothing of us in order to be completed. When the good Samaritan saw the traveller lying wounded and half dead, he did not tell him to get up, come over to him, climb on the donkey and ride off to the inn. No, “he came where he was,” cared for him, lifted him onto the animal, and carried him to the inn. That is how the Lord Jesus deals with us in our low and wretched condition.

We have seen that God justifies; that He justifies the ungodly; and that He justifies them through faith in the precious blood of Jesus. Now we must see what condition these ungodly people are in when Jesus works out their salvation. Many awakened people are troubled not only about their sin but about their moral weakness. They have no strength to escape from the mud they have fallen into, or to keep out of it in the days that follow. They grieve not only over what they have done, but over what they cannot do. They feel powerless, helpless and spiritually lifeless. It may sound strange to say that they feel dead, but that is exactly how it is. In their own estimation they are incapable of anything good. They cannot travel the road to heaven, because their bones are broken. “None of the men of strength have found their hands”; in fact, they are “without strength.” Happily, it is written, as the proof of God’s love to us:

“When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

Here we see conscious helplessness rescued — rescued by the intervention of the Lord Jesus. Our helplessness is extreme. It is not written, “When we were comparatively weak, Christ died for us,” or, “When we had only a little strength.” The description is absolute and without limit: “When we were yet without strength.” We had no strength at all that could help in our salvation. Our Lord’s words were emphatically true: “Without me ye can do nothing.” I can go further than the text, and remind you of the great love with which the Lord loved us, “even when we were dead in trespasses and sins.” To be dead is even more than to be without strength.

The one thing the poor, strengthless sinner has to fix his mind on, and hold on to firmly as his only ground of hope, is God’s assurance that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Believe this, and all inability will disappear. The legend says that Midas turned everything into gold by touching it; and it is true of faith that it turns everything it touches into good. Our very needs and weaknesses become blessings when faith deals with them.

Let us look at some particular forms of this lack of strength. To begin with, one man will say, “Sir, I don’t seem to have the strength to collect my thoughts and keep them fixed on the solemn subjects that concern my salvation. Even a short prayer is almost too much for me. Perhaps it is partly natural weakness, partly that I have damaged myself by loose living, and partly that I worry myself with worldly cares — so that I am not capable of the lofty thoughts that are necessary before a soul can be saved.” This is a very common form of sinful weakness. Notice this: you are without strength on this point, and there are many like you. They could not follow a connected train of thought to save their lives. Many poor men and women have had little schooling or training, and they would find deep thinking very heavy work. Others are so light and frivolous by nature that they could no more follow a long argument and line of reasoning than they could fly. They could never come to understand any profound mystery if they spent their whole lives trying. So you need not despair: what is necessary for salvation is not sustained thought, but simple reliance on Jesus. Hold on to this one fact: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” This truth will not require any deep research, profound reasoning or convincing argument from you. There it stands: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Fix your mind on that, and rest there.

Let this one great, gracious, glorious fact lie in your spirit until it perfumes all your thoughts and makes you rejoice even though you are without strength, since the Lord Jesus has become your strength and your song — yes, He has become your salvation. According to the Scriptures, it is a revealed fact that in due time Christ died for the ungodly when they were still without strength. You may have heard these words hundreds of times, and yet never before grasped their meaning. There is a cheering flavour about them, isn’t there? Jesus did not die for our righteousness; He died for our sins. He did not come to save us because we were worth saving, but because we were utterly worthless, ruined and lost. He did not come to earth for any reason found in us, but only and entirely for reasons He drew from the depths of His own divine love. In due time He died for those He describes, not as godly, but as ungodly — applying to them about as hopeless an adjective as He could have chosen. If you have only a small mind, fasten it to this truth anyway. It fits the smallest capacity and can cheer the heaviest heart. Let this text lie under your tongue like a sweet morsel until it melts into your heart and flavours all your thoughts; and then it will matter little if those thoughts are as scattered as autumn leaves. People who never shone in learning, or showed the least originality of mind, have still been fully able to accept the doctrine of the cross and be saved by it. Why shouldn’t you?

I hear another man cry, “Oh, sir, my lack of strength lies mainly in this — I cannot repent enough!” What a strange idea people have of repentance! Many imagine that so many tears must be shed, so many groans heaved, and so much despair endured. Where does this unreasonable notion come from? Unbelief and despair are sins, so I do not see how they can be essential ingredients of acceptable repentance; yet many people regard them as necessary parts of true Christian experience. They are greatly mistaken. Still, I know what they mean, for in my own days of darkness I used to feel the same. I wanted to repent, but I thought I could not, and all the while I was repenting. Strange as it may sound, I felt that I could not feel. I used to get into a corner and weep because I could not weep; and I fell into bitter sorrow because I could not sorrow for sin. What a muddle it all is when, in our state of unbelief, we start judging our own condition! It is like a blind man looking at his own eyes. My heart melted within me for fear, because I thought my heart was as hard as diamond. My heart was broken at the thought that it would not break. Now I can see that I was showing the very thing I thought I did not have; but at the time I did not know where I was.

Oh, that I could help others into the light I now enjoy! I would gladly say a word that might shorten their time of confusion. I will say a few plain words, and pray “the Comforter” to apply them to the heart.

Remember that a person who truly repents is never satisfied with his own repentance. We can no more repent perfectly than we can live perfectly. However pure our tears, there will always be some dirt in them; there will be something to repent of even in our best repentance. But listen! To repent is to change your mind about sin, and about Christ, and about all the great things of God. Sorrow is implied in this; but the main thing is the turning of the heart from sin to Christ. If there is this turning, you have the essence of true repentance, even if no alarm and no despair has ever cast its shadow over your mind.

If you cannot repent as you would like to, it will help you greatly to believe firmly that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Think about this again and again. How can you go on being hard-hearted when you know that, out of supreme love, “Christ died for the ungodly”? Let me persuade you to reason with yourself like this: “Ungodly as I am — though this heart of steel will not soften, though I beat my breast in vain — yet He died for people like me, since He died for the ungodly. Oh, that I may believe this and feel its power on my flinty heart!”

Wipe every other thought out of your soul, and sit down for hours together and meditate deeply on this one brilliant display of unearned, unexpected, unequalled love: “Christ died for the ungodly.” Read carefully through the account of the Lord’s death as you find it in the four Gospels. If anything can melt your stubborn heart, it will be the sight of the sufferings of Jesus, and the thought that He suffered all this for His enemies.

O Jesus! sweet the tears I shed, While at Thy feet I kneel,

Gaze on Thy wounded, fainting head, And all Thy sorrows feel.

My heart dissolves to see Thee bleed, This heart so hard before;

I hear Thee for the guilty plead, And grief o'erflows the more.

'Twas for the sinful Thou didst die, And I a sinner stand:

Convinc'd by Thine expiring eye, Slain by Thy pierced hand.

Surely the cross is that wonder-working rod that can bring water out of a rock. If you understand the full meaning of the divine sacrifice of Jesus, you must repent of ever having opposed One who is so full of love. It is written, “They shall look upon him whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.” Repentance will not make you see Christ; but seeing Christ will give you repentance. You must not make a Christ out of your repentance; you must look to Christ for repentance. The Holy Ghost, by turning us to Christ, turns us from sin. So look away from the effect to the cause — from your own repenting to the Lord Jesus, who is exalted on high to give repentance.

I have heard another person say, “I am tormented by horrible thoughts. Wherever I go, blasphemies creep in on me. Often at my work a dreadful suggestion forces itself on me, and even in bed I am startled out of my sleep by the whispers of the evil one. I cannot get away from this horrible temptation.” Friend, I know what you mean, for I have been hunted by this wolf myself. A man might as well hope to fight a swarm of flies with a sword as to master his own thoughts when the devil sets them on him. A poor tempted soul, attacked by satanic suggestions, is like a traveller I once read about, whose head and ears and whole body were covered by a swarm of angry bees. He could not keep them off or get away from them. They stung him everywhere and threatened to be the death of him. I am not surprised that you feel you have no strength to stop these hideous and abominable thoughts that Satan pours into your soul. But I would remind you of the Scripture before us: “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Jesus knew where we were and where we would be. He saw that we could not overcome the prince of the power of the air; He knew we would be badly harassed by him; but even then, when He saw us in that condition, Christ died for the ungodly. Drop the anchor of your faith here. The devil himself cannot tell you that you are not ungodly; so believe that Jesus died even for people like you. Remember Martin Luther’s way of cutting off the devil’s head with his own sword. “Oh,” said the devil to Martin Luther, “you are a sinner.” “Yes,” he said, “Christ died to save sinners.” So he struck him down with his own sword. Hide in this refuge and stay there: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If you stand by that truth, the blasphemous thoughts you have no strength to drive away will go away by themselves; for Satan will see that he is achieving nothing by plaguing you with them.

If you hate these thoughts, they are not yours at all; they are injections of the devil, and he is responsible for them, not you. If you fight against them, they are no more yours than the curses and lies of rioters in the street. The devil uses these thoughts to try to drive you to despair, or at least to keep you from trusting Jesus. The poor sick woman could not get to Jesus because of the crowd, and you are in much the same position because of the rush and crush of these dreadful thoughts. Still, she reached out her finger and touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment, and she was healed. Do the same.

Jesus died for those who are guilty of “all manner of sin and blasphemy,” so I am sure He will not refuse those who are unwilling captives of evil thoughts. Throw yourself on Him, thoughts and all, and see whether He is not mighty to save. He can silence those horrible whisperings of the fiend, or He can enable you to see them in their true light, so that you are not troubled by them. In His own way He can and will save you, and at last give you perfect peace. Only trust Him for this and for everything else.

Sadly bewildering is the form of inability that consists in a supposed lack of power to believe. We are no strangers to the cry:

Oh that I could believe,
Then all would easy be;
I would, but cannot; Lord, relieve,
My help must come from thee.

Many people stay in the dark for years because, as they say, they have no power to do the very thing that consists in giving up all power and resting in the power of another — the Lord Jesus. Indeed, this whole matter of believing is a very curious thing; for people do not get much help by trying to believe. Believing does not come by trying. If someone told me about something that happened today, I would not tell him I would try to believe him. If I trusted the truthfulness of the man who told me and said he saw it, I would accept what he said at once. If I did not think him an honest man, I would of course disbelieve him; but there would be no trying involved. Now, when God declares that there is salvation in Christ Jesus, I must either believe Him at once or make Him a liar. Surely you will not hesitate over which is the right path in this case. The witness of God must be true, and we are bound to believe in Jesus at once.

But perhaps you have been trying to believe too much. Do not aim at great things. Be content to have a faith that can hold in its hand this one truth: “While we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” He laid down His life for people while they were not yet believing in Him and were not able to believe in Him. He died for people, not as believers, but as sinners. He came to make these sinners into believers and saints; but when He died for them, He saw them as completely without strength. If you hold to the truth that Christ died for the ungodly, and believe it, your faith will save you, and you may go in peace. If you will trust your soul to Jesus, who died for the ungodly, then even though you cannot believe all things, or move mountains, or do any other wonderful works, you are saved. It is not great faith but true faith that saves; and the salvation lies not in the faith, but in the Christ whom faith trusts. Faith as a grain of mustard seed will bring salvation. What matters is not the size of faith but its sincerity. Surely a person can believe what he knows to be true; and since you know Jesus to be true, you, my friend, can believe in Him.

The cross, which is the object of faith, is also — by the power of the Holy Spirit — the cause of it. Sit down and watch the dying Saviour until faith springs up of its own accord in your heart. There is no place like Calvary for creating confidence. The air of that sacred hill brings health to trembling faith. Many who have watched there have said:

While I view Thee, wounded, grieving, Breathless on the cursed tree,

Lord, I feel my heart believing That Thou suffer'dst thus for me.

“Alas!” cries another, “my lack of strength is in this direction: I cannot give up my sin, and I know I cannot go to heaven and take my sin with me.” I am glad you know that, because it is quite true. You must be divorced from your sin, or you cannot be married to Christ. Remember the question that flashed into young Bunyan’s mind while he was at his games on the village green on a Sunday: “Wilt thou have thy sins and go to hell, or wilt thou quit thy sins and go to heaven?” That stopped him dead. It is a question every person will have to answer; for there is no going on in sin and going to heaven. That cannot be. You must give up sin or give up hope. Do you reply, “Yes, I am willing enough. To will is present with me, but how to perform that which I would I find not. Sin masters me, and I have no strength”? Come, then: if you have no strength, this text is still true, “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Can you still believe that? However much other things may seem to contradict it, will you believe it? God has said it, and it is a fact; so hold on to it like grim death, for your only hope lies there. Believe this and trust Jesus, and you will soon find the power to slay your sin; but apart from Him, the strong man armed will keep you as his slave for ever. Speaking for myself, I could never have overcome my own sinfulness. I tried and failed. My evil inclinations were too much for me, until, believing that Christ died for me, I threw my guilty soul on Him. Then I received a conquering principle by which I overcame my sinful self. The doctrine of the cross can be used to slay sin, just as the old warriors used their huge two-handed swords and mowed down their enemies at every stroke. There is nothing like faith in the sinner’s Friend: it overcomes all evil. If Christ has died for me, ungodly as I am, without strength as I am, then I cannot live in sin any longer, but must rouse myself to love and serve Him who has redeemed me. I cannot play around with the evil that killed my best Friend. I must be holy for His sake. How can I live in sin when He has died to save me from it?

See what a splendid help it is to you who are without strength to know and believe that in due time Christ died for ungodly people like you. Have you grasped the idea yet? Somehow it is so hard for our darkened, prejudiced and unbelieving minds to see the heart of the gospel. Sometimes, when I have finished preaching, I have thought that I set out the gospel so clearly that it could not have been plainer than the nose on your face; and yet I find that even intelligent listeners have not understood what was meant by “Look unto me and be ye saved.” Converts usually say that they did not know the gospel until such-and-such a day; and yet they had been hearing it for years. The gospel goes unknown, not for lack of explanation, but for lack of personal revelation. The Holy Ghost is ready to give this, and will give it to those who ask Him. Yet when it is given, the whole of the truth revealed lies within these words: “Christ died for the ungodly.”

I hear another person lamenting like this: “Oh, sir, my weakness is that I don’t seem to stay of one mind for long! I hear the word on a Sunday, and I am moved; but during the week I meet a bad companion, and my good feelings are all gone. My workmates don’t believe in anything, and they say such terrible things. I don’t know how to answer them, and so I find myself knocked flat.” I know this pliable, putty-like Mr. Pliable very well, and I tremble for him. But at the same time, if he is really sincere, divine grace can meet his weakness. The Holy Spirit can cast out the evil spirit of the fear of man. He can make the coward brave. Remember, my poor wavering friend, you must not stay in this state. It will never do to be mean and spineless toward yourself. Stand up straight, look at yourself, and ask whether you were ever meant to be like a toad under a harrow, afraid for your life either to move or to stay still. Do have a mind of your own. This is not only a spiritual matter; it is a matter of ordinary manliness. I would do many things to please my friends; but going to hell to please them is more than I would risk. It may be all very well to do this and that for the sake of good company; but it will never do to lose the friendship of God in order to stay on good terms with people. “I know that,” the man says, “but even though I know it, I can’t pluck up the courage. I can’t show my colours. I can’t stand firm.” Well, I have the same text for you too: “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If Peter were here, he would say, “The Lord Jesus died for me even when I was such a poor weak creature that the servant girl who kept the fire drove me to lie, and to swear that I did not know the Lord.” Yes, Jesus died for those who deserted Him and ran away. Take a firm grip on this truth: “Christ died for the ungodly while they were yet without strength.” This is your way out of your cowardice. Get this worked deep into your soul — “Christ died for me” — and you will soon be ready to die for Him. Believe that He suffered in your place, and offered for you a full, true and satisfying atonement. If you believe that fact, you will be compelled to feel, “I cannot be ashamed of Him who died for me.” A full conviction that this is true will brace you with fearless courage. Look at the saints in the age of the martyrs. In the early days of Christianity, when this great thought of Christ’s surpassing love was sparkling in all its freshness in the church, people were not only ready to die, but became eager to suffer, and even presented themselves by the hundreds at the rulers’ judgment seats, confessing Christ. I do not say they were wise to seek a cruel death; but it proves my point, that a sense of the love of Jesus lifts the mind above all fear of what people can do to us. Why shouldn’t it have the same effect on you? Oh, that it might inspire you now with a brave resolve to come out on the Lord’s side and follow Him to the end!

May the Holy Spirit help us to come this far by faith in the Lord Jesus, and all will be well!

The one thing the poor, strengthless sinner has to fix his mind on, and hold on to firmly as his only ground of hope, is God’s assurance that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Believe this, and all inability will disappear. The legend says that Midas turned everything into gold by touching it; and it is true of faith that it turns everything it touches into good. Our very needs and weaknesses become blessings when faith deals with them. Let us look at some particular forms of this lack of strength. To begin with, one man will say, “Sir, I don’t seem to have the strength to collect my thoughts and keep them fixed on the solemn subjects that concern my salvation. Even a short prayer is almost too much for me. Perhaps it is partly natural weakness, partly that I have damaged myself by loose living, and partly that I worry myself with worldly cares — so that I am not capable of the lofty thoughts that are necessary before a soul can be saved.” This is a very common form of sinful weakness. Notice this: you are without strength on this point, and there are many like you. They could not follow a connected train of thought to save their lives. Many poor men and women have had little schooling or training, and they would find deep thinking very heavy work. Others are so light and frivolous by nature that they could no more follow a long argument and line of reasoning than they could fly. They could never come to understand any profound mystery if they spent their whole lives trying. So you need not despair: what is necessary for salvation is not sustained thought, but simple reliance on Jesus. Hold on to this one fact: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” This truth will not require any deep research, profound reasoning or convincing argument from you. There it stands: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Fix your mind on that, and rest there. Let this one great, gracious, glorious fact lie in your spirit until it perfumes all your thoughts and makes you rejoice even though you are without strength, since the Lord Jesus has become your strength and your song — yes, He has become your salvation. According to the Scriptures, it is a revealed fact that in due time Christ died for the ungodly when they were still without strength. You may have heard these words hundreds of times, and yet never before grasped their meaning. There is a cheering flavour about them, isn’t there? Jesus did not die for our righteousness; He died for our sins. He did not come to save us because we were worth saving, but because we were utterly worthless, ruined and lost. He did not come to earth for any reason found in us, but only and entirely for reasons He drew from the depths of His own divine love. In due time He died for those He describes, not as godly, but as ungodly — applying to them about as hopeless an adjective as He could have chosen. If you have only a small mind, fasten it to this truth anyway. It fits the smallest capacity and can cheer the heaviest heart. Let this text lie under your tongue like a sweet morsel until it melts into your heart and flavours all your thoughts; and then it will matter little if those thoughts are as scattered as autumn leaves. People who never shone in learning, or showed the least originality of mind, have still been fully able to accept the doctrine of the cross and be saved by it. Why shouldn’t you? I hear another man cry, “Oh, sir, my lack of strength lies mainly in this — I cannot repent enough!” What a strange idea people have of repentance! Many imagine that so many tears must be shed, so many groans heaved, and so much despair endured. Where does this unreasonable notion come from? Unbelief and despair are sins, so I do not see how they can be essential ingredients of acceptable repentance; yet many people regard them as necessary parts of true Christian experience. They are greatly mistaken. Still, I know what they mean, for in my own days of darkness I used to feel the same. I wanted to repent, but I thought I could not, and all the while I was repenting. Strange as it may sound, I felt that I could not feel. I used to get into a corner and weep because I could not weep; and I fell into bitter sorrow because I could not sorrow for sin. What a muddle it all is when, in our state of unbelief, we start judging our own condition! It is like a blind man looking at his own eyes. My heart melted within me for fear, because I thought my heart was as hard as diamond. My heart was broken at the thought that it would not break. Now I can see that I was showing the very thing I thought I did not have; but at the time I did not know where I was. Oh, that I could help others into the light I now enjoy! I would gladly say a word that might shorten their time of confusion. I will say a few plain words, and pray “the Comforter” to apply them to the heart. Remember that a person who truly repents is never satisfied with his own repentance. We can no more repent perfectly than we can live perfectly. However pure our tears, there will always be some dirt in them; there will be something to repent of even in our best repentance. But listen! To repent is to change your mind about sin, and about Christ, and about all the great things of God. Sorrow is implied in this; but the main thing is the turning of the heart from sin to Christ. If there is this turning, you have the essence of true repentance, even if no alarm and no despair has ever cast its shadow over your mind. If you cannot repent as you would like to, it will help you greatly to believe firmly that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Think about this again and again. How can you go on being hard-hearted when you know that, out of supreme love, “Christ died for the ungodly”? Let me persuade you to reason with yourself like this: “Ungodly as I am — though this heart of steel will not soften, though I beat my breast in vain — yet He died for people like me, since He died for the ungodly. Oh, that I may believe this and feel its power on my flinty heart!” Wipe every other thought out of your soul, and sit down for hours together and meditate deeply on this one brilliant display of unearned, unexpected, unequalled love: “Christ died for the ungodly.” Read carefully through the account of the Lord’s death as you find it in the four Gospels. If anything can melt your stubborn heart, it will be the sight of the sufferings of Jesus, and the thought that He suffered all this for His enemies. O Jesus! sweet the tears I shed, While at Thy feet I kneel, Gaze on Thy wounded, fainting head, And all Thy sorrows feel. My heart dissolves to see Thee bleed, This heart so hard before; I hear Thee for the guilty plead, And grief o'erflows the more. 'Twas for the sinful Thou didst die, And I a sinner stand: Convinc'd by Thine expiring eye, Slain by Thy pierced hand. Surely the cross is that wonder-working rod that can bring water out of a rock. If you understand the full meaning of the divine sacrifice of Jesus, you must repent of ever having opposed One who is so full of love. It is written, “They shall look upon him whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.” Repentance will not make you see Christ; but seeing Christ will give you repentance. You must not make a Christ out of your repentance; you must look to Christ for repentance. The Holy Ghost, by turning us to Christ, turns us from sin. So look away from the effect to the cause — from your own repenting to the Lord Jesus, who is exalted on high to give repentance. I have heard another person say, “I am tormented by horrible thoughts. Wherever I go, blasphemies creep in on me. Often at my work a dreadful suggestion forces itself on me, and even in bed I am startled out of my sleep by the whispers of the evil one. I cannot get away from this horrible temptation.” Friend, I know what you mean, for I have been hunted by this wolf myself. A man might as well hope to fight a swarm of flies with a sword as to master his own thoughts when the devil sets them on him. A poor tempted soul, attacked by satanic suggestions, is like a traveller I once read about, whose head and ears and whole body were covered by a swarm of angry bees. He could not keep them off or get away from them. They stung him everywhere and threatened to be the death of him. I am not surprised that you feel you have no strength to stop these hideous and abominable thoughts that Satan pours into your soul. But I would remind you of the Scripture before us: “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Jesus knew where we were and where we would be. He saw that we could not overcome the prince of the power of the air; He knew we would be badly harassed by him; but even then, when He saw us in that condition, Christ died for the ungodly. Drop the anchor of your faith here. The devil himself cannot tell you that you are not ungodly; so believe that Jesus died even for people like you. Remember Martin Luther’s way of cutting off the devil’s head with his own sword. “Oh,” said the devil to Martin Luther, “you are a sinner.” “Yes,” he said, “Christ died to save sinners.” So he struck him down with his own sword. Hide in this refuge and stay there: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If you stand by that truth, the blasphemous thoughts you have no strength to drive away will go away by themselves; for Satan will see that he is achieving nothing by plaguing you with them. If you hate these thoughts, they are not yours at all; they are injections of the devil, and he is responsible for them, not you. If you fight against them, they are no more yours than the curses and lies of rioters in the street. The devil uses these thoughts to try to drive you to despair, or at least to keep you from trusting Jesus. The poor sick woman could not get to Jesus because of the crowd, and you are in much the same position because of the rush and crush of these dreadful thoughts. Still, she reached out her finger and touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment, and she was healed. Do the same. Jesus died for those who are guilty of “all manner of sin and blasphemy,” so I am sure He will not refuse those who are unwilling captives of evil thoughts. Throw yourself on Him, thoughts and all, and see whether He is not mighty to save. He can silence those horrible whisperings of the fiend, or He can enable you to see them in their true light, so that you are not troubled by them. In His own way He can and will save you, and at last give you perfect peace. Only trust Him for this and for everything else. Sadly bewildering is the form of inability that consists in a supposed lack of power to believe. We are no strangers to the cry: Oh that I could believe, Then all would easy be; I would, but cannot; Lord, relieve, My help must come from thee. Many people stay in the dark for years because, as they say, they have no power to do the very thing that consists in giving up all power and resting in the power of another — the Lord Jesus. Indeed, this whole matter of believing is a very curious thing; for people do not get much help by trying to believe. Believing does not come by trying. If someone told me about something that happened today, I would not tell him I would try to believe him. If I trusted the truthfulness of the man who told me and said he saw it, I would accept what he said at once. If I did not think him an honest man, I would of course disbelieve him; but there would be no trying involved. Now, when God declares that there is salvation in Christ Jesus, I must either believe Him at once or make Him a liar. Surely you will not hesitate over which is the right path in this case. The witness of God must be true, and we are bound to believe in Jesus at once. But perhaps you have been trying to believe too much. Do not aim at great things. Be content to have a faith that can hold in its hand this one truth: “While we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” He laid down His life for people while they were not yet believing in Him and were not able to believe in Him. He died for people, not as believers, but as sinners. He came to make these sinners into believers and saints; but when He died for them, He saw them as completely without strength. If you hold to the truth that Christ died for the ungodly, and believe it, your faith will save you, and you may go in peace. If you will trust your soul to Jesus, who died for the ungodly, then even though you cannot believe all things, or move mountains, or do any other wonderful works, you are saved. It is not great faith but true faith that saves; and the salvation lies not in the faith, but in the Christ whom faith trusts. Faith as a grain of mustard seed will bring salvation. What matters is not the size of faith but its sincerity. Surely a person can believe what he knows to be true; and since you know Jesus to be true, you, my friend, can believe in Him. The cross, which is the object of faith, is also — by the power of the Holy Spirit — the cause of it. Sit down and watch the dying Saviour until faith springs up of its own accord in your heart. There is no place like Calvary for creating confidence. The air of that sacred hill brings health to trembling faith. Many who have watched there have said: While I view Thee, wounded, grieving, Breathless on the cursed tree, Lord, I feel my heart believing That Thou suffer'dst thus for me. “Alas!” cries another, “my lack of strength is in this direction: I cannot give up my sin, and I know I cannot go to heaven and take my sin with me.” I am glad you know that, because it is quite true. You must be divorced from your sin, or you cannot be married to Christ. Remember the question that flashed into young Bunyan’s mind while he was at his games on the village green on a Sunday: “Wilt thou have thy sins and go to hell, or wilt thou quit thy sins and go to heaven?” That stopped him dead. It is a question every person will have to answer; for there is no going on in sin and going to heaven. That cannot be. You must give up sin or give up hope. Do you reply, “Yes, I am willing enough. To will is present with me, but how to perform that which I would I find not. Sin masters me, and I have no strength”? Come, then: if you have no strength, this text is still true, “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Can you still believe that? However much other things may seem to contradict it, will you believe it? God has said it, and it is a fact; so hold on to it like grim death, for your only hope lies there. Believe this and trust Jesus, and you will soon find the power to slay your sin; but apart from Him, the strong man armed will keep you as his slave for ever. Speaking for myself, I could never have overcome my own sinfulness. I tried and failed. My evil inclinations were too much for me, until, believing that Christ died for me, I threw my guilty soul on Him. Then I received a conquering principle by which I overcame my sinful self. The doctrine of the cross can be used to slay sin, just as the old warriors used their huge two-handed swords and mowed down their enemies at every stroke. There is nothing like faith in the sinner’s Friend: it overcomes all evil. If Christ has died for me, ungodly as I am, without strength as I am, then I cannot live in sin any longer, but must rouse myself to love and serve Him who has redeemed me. I cannot play around with the evil that killed my best Friend. I must be holy for His sake. How can I live in sin when He has died to save me from it? See what a splendid help it is to you who are without strength to know and believe that in due time Christ died for ungodly people like you. Have you grasped the idea yet? Somehow it is so hard for our darkened, prejudiced and unbelieving minds to see the heart of the gospel. Sometimes, when I have finished preaching, I have thought that I set out the gospel so clearly that it could not have been plainer than the nose on your face; and yet I find that even intelligent listeners have not understood what was meant by “Look unto me and be ye saved.” Converts usually say that they did not know the gospel until such-and-such a day; and yet they had been hearing it for years. The gospel goes unknown, not for lack of explanation, but for lack of personal revelation. The Holy Ghost is ready to give this, and will give it to those who ask Him. Yet when it is given, the whole of the truth revealed lies within these words: “Christ died for the ungodly.” I hear another person lamenting like this: “Oh, sir, my weakness is that I don’t seem to stay of one mind for long! I hear the word on a Sunday, and I am moved; but during the week I meet a bad companion, and my good feelings are all gone. My workmates don’t believe in anything, and they say such terrible things. I don’t know how to answer them, and so I find myself knocked flat.” I know this pliable, putty-like Mr. Pliable very well, and I tremble for him. But at the same time, if he is really sincere, divine grace can meet his weakness. The Holy Spirit can cast out the evil spirit of the fear of man. He can make the coward brave. Remember, my poor wavering friend, you must not stay in this state. It will never do to be mean and spineless toward yourself. Stand up straight, look at yourself, and ask whether you were ever meant to be like a toad under a harrow, afraid for your life either to move or to stay still. Do have a mind of your own. This is not only a spiritual matter; it is a matter of ordinary manliness. I would do many things to please my friends; but going to hell to please them is more than I would risk. It may be all very well to do this and that for the sake of good company; but it will never do to lose the friendship of God in order to stay on good terms with people. “I know that,” the man says, “but even though I know it, I can’t pluck up the courage. I can’t show my colours. I can’t stand firm.” Well, I have the same text for you too: “When we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If Peter were here, he would say, “The Lord Jesus died for me even when I was such a poor weak creature that the servant girl who kept the fire drove me to lie, and to swear that I did not know the Lord.” Yes, Jesus died for those who deserted Him and ran away. Take a firm grip on this truth: “Christ died for the ungodly while they were yet without strength.” This is your way out of your cowardice. Get this worked deep into your soul — “Christ died for me” — and you will soon be ready to die for Him. Believe that He suffered in your place, and offered for you a full, true and satisfying atonement. If you believe that fact, you will be compelled to feel, “I cannot be ashamed of Him who died for me.” A full conviction that this is true will brace you with fearless courage. Look at the saints in the age of the martyrs. In the early days of Christianity, when this great thought of Christ’s surpassing love was sparkling in all its freshness in the church, people were not only ready to die, but became eager to suffer, and even presented themselves by the hundreds at the rulers’ judgment seats, confessing Christ. I do not say they were wise to seek a cruel death; but it proves my point, that a sense of the love of Jesus lifts the mind above all fear of what people can do to us. Why shouldn’t it have the same effect on you? Oh, that it might inspire you now with a brave resolve to come out on the Lord’s side and follow Him to the end! May the Holy Spirit help us to come this far by faith in the Lord Jesus, and all will be well!

fields.title: The Increase of Faith
fields.body_html:
HOW CAN WE GET an increase of faith? For many people this is a very serious question. They say they want to believe, but cannot. A great deal of nonsense is talked on this subject. Let us be strictly practical about it. Common sense is needed in religion as much as anywhere else. “What am I to do in order to believe?” Someone who was asked the best way to do a certain simple thing answered that the best way to do it was to do it at once. We waste time discussing methods when the action is simple. The shortest way to believe is to believe. If the Holy Spirit has made you honest, you will believe as soon as the truth is set before you. You will believe it because it is true. The gospel command is clear: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved.” It is pointless to dodge this with questions and quibbles. The order is plain; let it be obeyed.

But if you still have difficulty, take it to God in prayer. Tell the great Father exactly what puzzles you, and beg Him by His Holy Spirit to settle the question. If I cannot believe a statement in a book, I am glad to ask the author what he means by it; and if he is an honest man, his explanation will satisfy me. How much more will God’s own explanation of the hard points of Scripture satisfy the heart of the true seeker! The Lord is willing to make Himself known; go to Him and see if it is not so. Go at once to your private room and cry, “O Holy Spirit, lead me into the truth! What I know not, teach Thou me.”

Furthermore, if faith seems difficult, it may be that God the Holy Spirit will enable you to believe if you hear, very often and very earnestly, what you are commanded to believe. We believe many things because we have heard them so often. Don’t you find in everyday life that if you hear something fifty times a day, you end up believing it? Some people have come to believe very unlikely statements this way; so I am not surprised that the good Spirit often blesses the practice of hearing the truth often, and uses it to work faith in what is to be believed. It is written, “Faith cometh by hearing”; so hear often. If I listen earnestly and attentively to the gospel, one of these days I will find myself believing what I hear, through the blessed work of the Spirit of God on my mind. Only make sure it is the gospel you hear, and do not distract your mind by hearing or reading things designed to shake you.

If that seems poor advice, I would add this next: consider the testimony of others. The Samaritans believed because of what the woman told them about Jesus. Many of our beliefs come from the testimony of others. I believe there is such a country as Japan. I have never seen it, yet I believe there is such a place because others have been there. I believe that I will die. I have never died, but a great many people I once knew have, and so I am convinced that I will die too. The testimony of many convinces me of that fact. So listen to those who tell you how they were saved, how they were pardoned, how their character was changed. If you look into it, you will find that someone just like you has been saved. If you have been a thief, you will find that a thief rejoiced to wash away his sin in the fountain of Christ’s blood. If, sadly, you have been sexually immoral, you will find that men and women who have fallen in that way have been cleansed and changed. If you are in despair, you only have to go among God’s people and ask a few questions, and you will discover that some of the saints have been in just as much despair at times; and they will be glad to tell you how the Lord rescued them. As you listen to one after another of those who have tried the Word of God and proved it true, the divine Spirit will lead you to believe. Have you heard of the African man whom the missionary told that water sometimes became so hard that a person could walk on it? He declared that he believed a great many things the missionary had told him, but he would never believe that. When he came to England, it happened that one frosty day he saw the river frozen; but he would not venture onto it. He knew it was a deep river, and he felt sure he would drown if he stepped onto it. Nothing could persuade him to walk on the frozen water until his friend and many others went onto it. Then he was convinced, and trusted himself where others had safely gone. In the same way, as you see others believe in the Lamb of God, and notice their joy and peace, you yourself will be gently led to believe. The experience of others is one of God’s ways of helping us to faith. You must either believe in Jesus or die; there is no hope for you except in Him.

A better plan is this: notice the authority on which you are commanded to believe, and this will help you greatly toward faith. The authority is not mine, or you might well reject it. You are commanded to believe on the authority of God Himself. He tells you to believe in Jesus Christ, and you must not refuse to obey your Maker. The foreman of a certain factory had often heard the gospel, but he was troubled by the fear that he might not come to Christ. One day his good employer sent a card round to the factory: “Come to my house immediately after work.” The foreman turned up at his employer’s door, and the employer came out and said rather roughly, “What do you want, John, bothering me at this hour? Work is over — what right have you to be here?” “Sir,” he said, “I had a card from you saying I was to come after work.” “Do you mean to say that just because you had a card from me, you can come up to my house and call me out after business hours?” “Well, sir,” replied the foreman, “I don’t understand you; but it seems to me that since you sent for me, I had a right to come.” “Come in, John,” said his employer. “I have another message I want to read to you.” He sat down and read these words: “Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” “After a message like that from Christ, do you think you can be wrong in coming to Him?” The poor man saw it all at once, and believed in the Lord Jesus unto eternal life, because he realised he had good warrant and authority for believing. So do you, poor soul! You have good authority for coming to Christ, for the Lord Himself tells you to trust Him.

If that does not produce faith in you, think about what it is you have to believe: that the Lord Jesus Christ suffered in the place of sinners, and is able to save all who trust Him. Why, this is the most blessed fact anyone was ever told to believe — the most fitting, the most comforting, the most divine truth ever set before mortal minds. I advise you to think about it a great deal, and search out the grace and love it contains. Study the four Gospels, study Paul’s letters, and then see whether the message is not so believable that you are compelled to believe it.

If that does not work, then think about the person of Jesus Christ — think about who He is, what He did, where He is, and what He is. How can you doubt Him? It is cruel to distrust the ever-truthful Jesus. He has done nothing to deserve distrust; on the contrary, it should be easy to rely on Him. Why crucify Him afresh by unbelief? Isn’t this crowning Him with thorns again, and spitting on Him again? What! Is He not to be trusted? What worse insult did the soldiers heap on Him than this? They made Him a martyr; but you make Him a liar — and that is far worse. Do not ask, “How can I believe?” Answer another question instead: “How can you disbelieve?”

If none of these things helps, then something is wrong with you at a deeper level, and my last word is this: submit yourself to God! Prejudice or pride lies at the bottom of this unbelief. May the Spirit of God take away your hostility and make you yield. You are a rebel, a proud rebel, and that is why you do not believe your God. Give up your rebellion; throw down your weapons; surrender unconditionally to your King. I believe that no soul ever threw up its hands in self-despair and cried, “Lord, I yield,” without finding before long that faith became easy. It is because you still have a quarrel with God, and are determined to have your own will and your own way, that you cannot believe. “How can ye believe,” said Christ, “that have honor one of another?” Proud self breeds unbelief. Submit, O man. Yield to your God, and then you will sweetly believe in your Saviour. May the Holy Ghost now work in you, quietly but effectively, and bring you at this very moment to believe in the Lord Jesus! Amen.

A better plan is this: notice the authority on which you are commanded to believe, and this will help you greatly toward faith. The authority is not mine, or you might well reject it. You are commanded to believe on the authority of God Himself. He tells you to believe in Jesus Christ, and you must not refuse to obey your Maker. The foreman of a certain factory had often heard the gospel, but he was troubled by the fear that he might not come to Christ. One day his good employer sent a card round to the factory: “Come to my house immediately after work.” The foreman turned up at his employer’s door, and the employer came out and said rather roughly, “What do you want, John, bothering me at this hour? Work is over — what right have you to be here?” “Sir,” he said, “I had a card from you saying I was to come after work.” “Do you mean to say that just because you had a card from me, you can come up to my house and call me out after business hours?” “Well, sir,” replied the foreman, “I don’t understand you; but it seems to me that since you sent for me, I had a right to come.” “Come in, John,” said his employer. “I have another message I want to read to you.” He sat down and read these words: “Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” “After a message like that from Christ, do you think you can be wrong in coming to Him?” The poor man saw it all at once, and believed in the Lord Jesus unto eternal life, because he realised he had good warrant and authority for believing. Why, this is the most blessed fact anyone was ever told to believe — the most fitting, the most comforting, the most divine truth ever set before mortal minds. I advise you to think about it a great deal, and search out the grace and love it contains. Study the four Gospels, study Paul’s letters, and then see whether the message is not so believable that you are compelled to believe it. It is cruel to distrust the ever-truthful Jesus. He has done nothing to deserve distrust; on the contrary, it should be easy to rely on Him. Why crucify Him afresh by unbelief? Isn’t this crowning Him with thorns again, and spitting on Him again? What! Is He not to be trusted? What worse insult did the soldiers heap on Him than this? They made Him a martyr; but you make Him a liar — and that is far worse. Do not ask, “How can I believe?” Answer another question instead: “How can you disbelieve?” If none of these things helps, then something is wrong with you at a deeper level, and my last word is this: submit yourself to God! Prejudice or pride lies at the bottom of this unbelief. May the Spirit of God take away your hostility and make you yield. You are a rebel, a proud rebel, and that is why you do not believe your God. Give up your rebellion; throw down your weapons; surrender unconditionally to your King. I believe that no soul ever threw up its hands in self-despair and cried, “Lord, I yield,” without finding before long that faith became easy. It is because you still have a quarrel with God, and are determined to have your own will and your own way, that you cannot believe. “How can ye believe,” said Christ, “that have honor one of another?” Proud self breeds unbelief. Submit, O man. Yield to your God, and then you will sweetly believe in your Saviour. May the Holy Ghost now work in you, quietly but effectively, and bring you at this very moment to believe in the Lord Jesus! Amen.

fields.title: Regeneration and the Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
“YE MUST BE BORN AGAIN.” For many people this word of our Lord Jesus has seemed to blaze across their path like the drawn sword of the cherub at the gate of Paradise. They have despaired, because this change is beyond their utmost effort. The new birth comes from above, and so it is not within the creature’s power. Now, I have no wish to deny, or ever to hide, any truth in order to create a false comfort. I freely admit that the new birth is supernatural, and that the sinner cannot bring it about by himself. It would be poor help to my reader if I were wicked enough to try to cheer him up by persuading him to reject or forget what is unquestionably true.

But isn’t it remarkable that the very chapter in which our Lord makes this sweeping declaration also contains the most explicit statement about salvation by faith? Read the third chapter of John’s Gospel, and do not dwell only on its opening sentences. It is true that the third verse says:

Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

But then the fourteenth and fifteenth verses say:

And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

The eighteenth verse repeats the same teaching in the broadest terms:

He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.

Every reader can see that these two statements must agree, since they came from the same lips and are recorded on the same inspired page. Why should we make a difficulty where there can be none? One statement assures us that something only God can give is necessary for salvation; another assures us that the Lord will save us when we believe in Jesus. So we may safely conclude that the Lord will give to those who believe everything that is declared to be necessary for salvation. In fact, the Lord does produce the new birth in all who believe in Jesus; and their believing is the surest evidence that they are born again.

We trust in Jesus for what we cannot do ourselves: if it were in our own power, why would we need to look to Him? Our part is to believe; it is the Lord’s part to create us anew. He will not believe for us, and we are not to do His work of regeneration for Him. It is enough for us to obey the gracious command; it is for the Lord to work the new birth in us. He who could go so far as to die on the cross for us can and will give us everything needed for our eternal safety.

“But a saving change of heart is the work of the Holy Spirit.” This is also perfectly true, and far be it from us to question it or forget it. But the work of the Holy Spirit is hidden and mysterious, and it can only be seen by its results. There are mysteries about our natural birth that it would be an unholy curiosity to pry into; this is even more true of the sacred workings of the Spirit of God. “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, or whither it goeth; so is every one that is born of the Spirit.” This much, however, we do know: the mysterious work of the Holy Spirit cannot be a reason for refusing to believe in Jesus, to whom that same Spirit bears witness.

If a man were told to sow a field, he could not excuse his neglect by saying it would be useless to sow unless God made the seed grow. He would not be justified in neglecting to till the ground just because only the secret power of God can create a harvest. No one is held back in the ordinary business of life by the fact that unless the Lord build the house they labor in vain that build it. It is certain that no one who believes in Jesus will ever find the Holy Spirit refusing to work in him; in fact, his believing is the proof that the Spirit is already at work in his heart.

God works in providence, but people do not sit still because of that. They could not move unless divine power gave them life and strength, and yet they go on their way without a second thought — the power being given day by day by Him in whose hand their breath is, and to whom all their ways belong. It is the same in grace. We repent and believe, though we could do neither if the Lord did not enable us. We forsake sin and trust in Jesus, and then we realise that the Lord has worked in us to will and to do of His own good pleasure. It is pointless to pretend there is any real difficulty here.

Some truths that are hard to explain in words are simple enough in actual experience. There is no contradiction between the truth that the sinner believes and the truth that his faith is worked in him by the Holy Spirit. Only folly can lead people to puzzle themselves over plain matters while their souls are in danger. No one would refuse to get into a lifeboat because he did not know the specific gravity of objects; and no starving man would refuse to eat until he understood the whole process of nutrition. If you, my reader, will not believe until you can understand every mystery, you will never be saved at all. And if you let difficulties you have invented yourself keep you from accepting pardon through your Lord and Saviour, you will perish under a condemnation you will richly deserve. Do not commit spiritual suicide out of a passion for debating philosophical subtleties.

fields.title: My Redeemer Lives
fields.body_html:
AGAIN AND AGAIN I have spoken to the reader about Christ crucified, who is the great hope of the guilty; but we would be wise to remember that our Lord has risen from the dead and lives for ever.

You are not asked to trust in a dead Jesus, but in One who, though He died for our sins, has risen again for our justification. You may go to Jesus at once as a living friend who is present with you. He is not a mere memory, but a Person who goes on living for ever, who will hear your prayers and answer them. He lives for the very purpose of carrying on the work for which He once laid down His life. He is interceding for sinners at the right hand of the Father, and that is why He is able to save them to the uttermost who come unto God by Him. Come and try this living Saviour, if you have never done so before.

This living Jesus has also been raised to a height of glory and power. He no longer grieves as “a humble man before his foes,” or toils as “the carpenter’s son”; He is exalted far above principalities and power and every name that is named. The Father has given Him all power in heaven and on earth, and He uses this high authority in carrying out His work of grace. Listen to what Peter and the other apostles testified about Him before the high priest and the council:

The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree. Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins (Acts 5:30, 31).

The glory that surrounds the ascended Lord should breathe hope into every believer’s heart. Jesus is no ordinary person — He is “a Saviour and a great one.” He is the crowned and enthroned Redeemer of men. The sovereign right over life and death belongs to Him. The Father has placed all people under the mediating rule of the Son, so that He can give life to whomever He wills. He openeth, and no man shutteth. At His word, the soul that is tied up by the cords of sin and condemnation can be set loose in a moment. He holds out the silver sceptre, and whoever touches it lives.

It is good for us that, just as sin lives, and the flesh lives, and the devil lives, so Jesus lives; and it is good too that, whatever power these may have to ruin us, Jesus has still greater power to save us.

All His exaltation and power are for our sake. “He is exalted to be,” and exalted “to give.” He is exalted to be a Prince and a Saviour, so that He may give everything needed to accomplish the salvation of all who come under His rule. Jesus has nothing that He will not use for a sinner’s salvation, and there is nothing He is that He will not display in the overflowing of His grace. He links His princely rule with His work as Saviour, as if He would not have one without the other; and He presents His exaltation as intended to bring blessings to people, as if this were the flower and crown of His glory. Could anything be better suited to raise the hopes of seeking sinners who are looking toward Christ?

Jesus endured great humiliation, and so there was room for Him to be exalted. Through that humiliation He accomplished and endured all the Father’s will, and so He was rewarded by being raised to glory. He uses that exaltation on behalf of His people. Let my reader lift his eyes to these hills of glory, from which his help must come. Let him gaze on the high glories of the Prince and Saviour. Isn’t it full of hope for us that a Man is now on the throne of the universe? Isn’t it glorious that the Lord of all is the Saviour of sinners? We have a Friend at court — yes, a Friend on the throne. He will use all His influence for those who place their affairs in His hands. One of our poets sings it well:

He ever lives to intercede

Before His Father's face;

Give Him, my soul, Thy cause to plead,

No doubt the Father's grace.

Come, friend, and commit your cause and your case to those once-pierced hands, which are now glorified with the signet rings of royal power and honour. No case ever failed that was left with this great Advocate.
