fields.title: Repentance Must Go with Forgiveness
fields.body_html:
IT IS CLEAR from the text we quoted a moment ago that repentance is bound up with the forgiveness of sins. In Acts 5:31 we read that Jesus is “exalted to give repentance and forgiveness of sins.” These two blessings come from that sacred hand which was once nailed to the tree but is now raised to glory. Repentance and forgiveness are riveted together by the eternal purpose of God. What God hath joined together let no man put asunder.

Repentance must go with forgiveness, and you will see that this is so if you think about it for a moment. Pardon for sin cannot be given to a sinner who will not repent; that would be to confirm him in his evil ways and teach him to think lightly of evil. If the Lord were to say, “You love sin, and live in it, and you are going from bad to worse — but all the same, I forgive you,” that would be to proclaim a horrible licence to sin. The foundations of social order would be removed, and moral chaos would follow. I cannot tell you what countless evils would certainly result if you could separate repentance and forgiveness, and overlook the sin while the sinner remained as fond of it as ever. If we believe in the holiness of God, it must be so by the very nature of things: if we go on in our sin and will not repent of it, we cannot be forgiven, but must reap the consequences of our stubbornness. In the infinite goodness of God, we are promised that if we will forsake our sins, confessing them, and will by faith accept the grace provided in Christ Jesus, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. But as long as God lives, there can be no promise of mercy to those who continue in their evil ways and refuse to admit their wrongdoing. Surely no rebel can expect the King to pardon his treason while he remains in open revolt. No one can be foolish enough to imagine that the Judge of all the earth will put away our sins if we refuse to put them away ourselves.

Moreover, it must be so for the sake of the completeness of God’s mercy. A mercy that could forgive the sin and yet let the sinner go on living in it would be a meagre and shallow mercy. It would be lopsided and deformed — lame in one foot and withered in one hand. Which do you think is the greater privilege: cleansing from the guilt of sin, or deliverance from the power of sin? I will not try to weigh two such surpassing mercies on the scales. Neither of them could have come to us without the precious blood of Jesus. But it seems to me that being set free from the rule of sin — being made holy, being made like God — must be counted the greater of the two, if we have to compare them. To be forgiven is a favour beyond measure. We make it one of the first notes of our psalm of praise: “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities.” But if we could be forgiven, and then be allowed to love sin, to run riot in wickedness and wallow in lust, what use would such forgiveness be? Might it not turn out to be a poisoned sweet that would destroy us all the more surely? To be washed and yet lie in the mud; to be declared clean and yet have the leprosy white on one’s forehead — that would be the cruellest mockery of mercy. What is the point of bringing a man out of his tomb if you leave him dead? Why lead him into the light if he is still blind? We thank God that He who forgives our iniquities also heals our diseases. He who washes us from the stains of the past also lifts us out of the foul ways of the present and keeps us from falling in the future. We must joyfully accept both repentance and forgiveness; they cannot be separated. The inheritance of the covenant is one and indivisible, and must not be split up. To divide the work of grace would be to cut the living child in two; and those who would allow that have no real share in it.

Let me ask you who are seeking the Lord: would you be satisfied with just one of these mercies? Would it content you, my reader, if God forgave your sin and then left you to be as worldly and wicked as before? Oh, no! The spirit that has been made alive is more afraid of sin itself than of its penalty. The cry of your heart is not, “Who will rescue me from punishment?” but, “O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Who will enable me to live above temptation and become holy, as God is holy?” Since the union of repentance with forgiveness matches the desires grace creates, and since it is necessary for the completeness of salvation and for the sake of holiness, you may rest assured that it stands firm.

Repentance and forgiveness are joined together in the experience of every believer. There has never yet been anyone who sincerely repented of sin with a believing repentance who was not forgiven; and on the other hand, there has never been anyone forgiven who had not repented of his sin. I do not hesitate to say that under the vault of heaven there never was, there is not, and there never will be any case of sin being washed away unless, at the same time, the heart was led to repentance and to faith in Christ. Hatred of sin and a sense of pardon come into the soul together, and stay together as long as we live.

These two things act on each other and feed each other. The person who is forgiven repents because of it; and the person who repents is most certainly forgiven. Remember first that forgiveness leads to repentance. As we sing in Hart’s words:

Law and terrors do but harden,
All the while they work alone;
But a sense of blood-bought pardon
Soon dissolves a heart of stone.

When we are sure we are forgiven, then we loathe sin. And I suppose that when faith grows into full assurance, so that we are certain beyond doubt that the blood of Jesus has washed us whiter than snow, that is when repentance reaches its greatest height. Repentance grows as faith grows. Make no mistake about it: repentance is not a matter of days and weeks, a temporary penance to be got over as fast as possible! No; like faith itself, it is the grace of a lifetime. God’s little children repent, and so do the young men and the fathers. Repentance is faith’s inseparable companion. All the while we walk by faith and not by sight, the tear of repentance glistens in the eye of faith. Repentance that does not come from faith in Jesus is not true repentance; and faith in Jesus that is not tinged with repentance is not true faith. Faith and repentance, like conjoined twins, are joined together at the very life. To the degree that we believe in the forgiving love of Christ, to that degree we repent; and to the degree that we repent of sin and hate evil, we rejoice in the fullness of the absolution Jesus is exalted to give. You will never value pardon unless you feel repentance; and you will never drink the deepest draught of repentance until you know you are pardoned. It may seem strange, but it is true: the bitterness of repentance and the sweetness of pardon blend in the flavour of every gracious life and make up a happiness beyond compare.

These two covenant gifts each assure us of the other. If I know that I repent, I know that I am forgiven. How am I to know I am forgiven unless I also know that I have turned from my former sinful course? To be a believer is to be a penitent. Faith and repentance are just two spokes in the same wheel, two handles of the same plough. Repentance has been well described as a heart broken for sin and from sin; and it could just as well be described as turning and returning. It is a change of mind of the most thorough and radical kind, and it comes with sorrow for the past and a resolve to do better in the future.

Repentance is to leave

The sins we loved before;

And show that we in earnest grieve,

By doing so no more.

Now, when that is the case, we may be certain we are forgiven; for the Lord never made a heart broken for sin and broken from sin without pardoning it. On the other hand, if we are enjoying pardon through the blood of Jesus, and are justified by faith, and have peace with God through Jesus Christ our Lord, then we know that our repentance and faith are the right kind.

Do not think of your repentance as the cause of your forgiveness, but as its companion. Do not expect to be able to repent until you see the grace of our Lord Jesus and His readiness to blot out your sin. Keep these blessed things in their proper places, and see how they relate to each other. They are the Jachin and Boaz of a saving experience — by which I mean they are like Solomon’s two great pillars that stood at the front of the house of the Lord and formed a majestic entrance to the holy place. No one comes to God rightly unless he passes between the pillars of repentance and forgiveness. The rainbow of covenant grace has been displayed in all its beauty on your heart when the light of full forgiveness has shone on the teardrops of repentance. Repentance of sin and faith in God’s pardon are the warp and weft of the fabric of real conversion. By these signs you will recognise an Israelite indeed.

To come back to the Scripture we are meditating on: both forgiveness and repentance flow from the same source and are given by the same Saviour. The Lord Jesus in His glory gives both to the same people. You will not find either the forgiveness or the repentance anywhere else. Jesus has both ready, and He is prepared to give them now, and to give them most freely to all who will accept them from His hands. Let us never forget that Jesus gives everything necessary for our salvation. It is very important that everyone seeking mercy should remember this. Faith is as much the gift of God as the Saviour on whom that faith relies. Repentance of sin is as truly the work of grace as the making of the atonement by which sin is blotted out. Salvation, from first to last, is by grace alone. You will not misunderstand me. It is not the Holy Spirit who repents. He has never done anything He should repent of. And if He could repent, it would not meet our case; we must repent of our own sin ourselves, or we are not saved from its power. It is not the Lord Jesus Christ who repents. What would He repent of? We ourselves repent, with the full consent of every faculty of our minds. The will, the affections, the emotions all work together wholeheartedly in the blessed act of repenting of sin; and yet behind all that is our own personal act, there is a secret, holy influence that melts the heart, gives contrition, and produces a complete change. The Spirit of God enlightens us to see what sin is, and so makes it loathsome in our eyes. The Spirit of God also turns us toward holiness, makes us truly value it, love it and desire it, and so gives us the drive that carries us on from stage to stage of sanctification. The Spirit of God works in us to will and to do according to God’s good pleasure. Let us submit ourselves to that good Spirit at once, so that He may lead us to Jesus, who will freely give us the double blessing of repentance and forgiveness, according to the riches of His grace.

“BY GRACE ARE YE SAVED.”

In Acts 5:31 we read that Jesus is “exalted to give repentance and forgiveness of sins.” These two blessings come from that sacred hand which was once nailed to the tree but is now raised to glory. Repentance and forgiveness are riveted together by the eternal purpose of God. What God hath joined together let no man put asunder. Repentance must go with forgiveness, and you will see that this is so if you think about it for a moment. Pardon for sin cannot be given to a sinner who will not repent; that would be to confirm him in his evil ways and teach him to think lightly of evil. If the Lord were to say, “You love sin, and live in it, and you are going from bad to worse — but all the same, I forgive you,” that would be to proclaim a horrible licence to sin. The foundations of social order would be removed, and moral chaos would follow. I cannot tell you what countless evils would certainly result if you could separate repentance and forgiveness, and overlook the sin while the sinner remained as fond of it as ever. If we believe in the holiness of God, it must be so by the very nature of things: if we go on in our sin and will not repent of it, we cannot be forgiven, but must reap the consequences of our stubbornness. In the infinite goodness of God, we are promised that if we will forsake our sins, confessing them, and will by faith accept the grace provided in Christ Jesus, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. But as long as God lives, there can be no promise of mercy to those who continue in their evil ways and refuse to admit their wrongdoing. Surely no rebel can expect the King to pardon his treason while he remains in open revolt. No one can be foolish enough to imagine that the Judge of all the earth will put away our sins if we refuse to put them away ourselves. Moreover, it must be so for the sake of the completeness of God’s mercy. A mercy that could forgive the sin and yet let the sinner go on living in it would be a meagre and shallow mercy. It would be lopsided and deformed — lame in one foot and withered in one hand. Which do you think is the greater privilege: cleansing from the guilt of sin, or deliverance from the power of sin? What is the point of bringing a man out of his tomb if you leave him dead? Why lead him into the light if he is still blind? We thank God that He who forgives our iniquities also heals our diseases. We must joyfully accept both repentance and forgiveness; they cannot be separated. The inheritance of the covenant is one and indivisible, and must not be split up. To divide the work of grace would be to cut the living child in two; and those who would allow that have no real share in it. Would it content you, my reader, if God forgave your sin and then left you to be as worldly and wicked as before? Oh, no! The spirit that has been made alive is more afraid of sin itself than of its penalty. The cry of your heart is not, “Who will rescue me from punishment?” but, “O wretched man that I am! The person who is forgiven repents because of it; and the person who repents is most certainly forgiven. Remember first that forgiveness leads to repentance. As we sing in Hart’s words: Law and terrors do but harden, All the while they work alone; But a sense of blood-bought pardon Soon dissolves a heart of stone. When we are sure we are forgiven, then we loathe sin. And I suppose that when faith grows into full assurance, so that we are certain beyond doubt that the blood of Jesus has washed us whiter than snow, that is when repentance reaches its greatest height. Repentance grows as faith grows. Make no mistake about it: repentance is not a matter of days and weeks, a temporary penance to be got over as fast as possible! No; like faith itself, it is the grace of a lifetime. God’s little children repent, and so do the young men and the fathers. Repentance is faith’s inseparable companion. fields.title: How Repentance Is Given
fields.body_html:
TO RETURN to our great text: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.” Our Lord Jesus Christ has gone up so that grace may come down. His glory is put to work to spread His grace all the more widely. The Lord has not taken a single step upward except with the aim of carrying believing sinners up with Him. He is exalted to give repentance; and we will see this if we remember a few great truths.

The work our Lord Jesus has done has made repentance possible, available and acceptable. The law says nothing about repentance; it says plainly, “The soul that sinneth, it shall die.” If the Lord Jesus had not died and risen again and gone to the Father, what would your repenting or mine be worth? We might feel remorse, with all its horrors, but never repentance, with its hopes. Repentance as a natural feeling is an ordinary duty that deserves no great praise. In fact, it is usually so mixed up with a selfish fear of punishment that even the kindest assessment makes little of it. If Jesus had not stepped in and worked out a wealth of merit, our tears of repentance would have been so much water spilled on the ground. Jesus is exalted on high so that, through the power of His intercession, repentance may have a place before God. In this sense He gives us repentance, because He puts repentance in a position of acceptance it could never otherwise have had.

When Jesus was exalted on high, the Spirit of God was poured out to work in us every grace we need. The Holy Ghost creates repentance in us by renewing our nature supernaturally and taking the heart of stone out of our flesh. Oh, do not sit there straining those eyes of yours to squeeze out impossible tears! Repentance does not come from unwilling nature, but from free and sovereign grace. Do not shut yourself in your room and beat your breast to try to wring from a heart of stone feelings that are not there. Instead, go to Calvary and see how Jesus died. Look up to the hills from which your help comes. The Holy Ghost has come for the very purpose of overshadowing people’s spirits and bringing repentance to birth in them, just as He once brooded over the chaos and brought order out of it. Breathe your prayer to Him: “Blessed Spirit, live in me. Make me tender and humble of heart, so that I may hate sin and sincerely repent of it.” He will hear your cry and answer you.

Remember too that when our Lord Jesus was exalted, He gave us repentance not only by sending the Holy Spirit, but also by dedicating all the works of nature and of providence to the great purposes of our salvation. So any one of them may call us to repentance — whether it crows like Peter’s rooster or shakes the prison like the jailer’s earthquake. From the right hand of God our Lord Jesus rules everything here below and makes it all work together for the salvation of His redeemed. He uses both bitter things and sweet, trials and joys, to produce in sinners a better attitude toward their God. Be thankful for the providence that has made you poor, or sick, or sad; for through all of this Jesus is working the life of your spirit and turning you to Himself. The Lord’s mercy often rides up to the door of our hearts on the black horse of affliction. Jesus uses the whole range of our experience to wean us from earth and woo us to heaven. Christ is exalted to the throne of heaven and earth so that, by all the workings of His providence, He may bring hard hearts under the gracious softening of repentance.

Besides, He is at work at this very hour — by all His whispers in the conscience, by His inspired Book, by those of us who speak from that Book, and by praying friends and earnest hearts. He can send you a word that will strike your rocky heart as Moses’ rod struck the rock, and make streams of repentance flow. He can bring to mind some heartbreaking text of Holy Scripture that will conquer you very quickly. He can soften you mysteriously, and make a holy frame of mind steal over you when you least expect it. Be sure of this: He who has gone into His glory, raised into all the splendour and majesty of God, has plenty of ways of working repentance in those to whom He grants forgiveness. He is waiting even now to give repentance to you. Ask Him for it at once.

Notice, and take great comfort from it, that the Lord Jesus Christ gives this repentance to the most unlikely people in the world. He is exalted to give repentance to Israel. To Israel! In the days when the apostles said this, Israel was the nation that had sinned most grossly against light and love, by daring to say, “His blood be on us and on our children.” Yet Jesus is exalted to give them repentance! What a marvel of grace! If you were brought up in the brightest Christian light and yet rejected it, there is still hope. If you have sinned against conscience, and against the Holy Spirit, and against the love of Jesus, there is still room for repentance. Though you may be as hard as unbelieving Israel of old, softening may yet come to you, since Jesus is exalted and clothed with boundless power. For those who have gone furthest in wickedness, and sinned with special aggravation, the Lord Jesus is exalted to give them repentance and forgiveness of sins. How happy I am to have so full a gospel to proclaim! How happy you are to be allowed to read it!

The hearts of the children of Israel had grown as hard as diamond. Luther used to think it impossible to convert a Jew. We are far from agreeing with him; and yet we must admit that the descendants of Israel have been extremely stubborn in rejecting the Saviour over these many centuries. The Lord spoke truly when He said, “Israel would none of me.” “He came to his own and his own received him not.” Yet on Israel’s behalf our Lord Jesus is exalted to give repentance and forgiveness. My reader is probably a Gentile; but he may still have a very stubborn heart that has held out against the Lord Jesus for many years — and yet our Lord can work repentance even in him. It may be that you too will one day feel compelled to write as William Hone did when he gave in to divine love. He was the author of those very entertaining volumes called the “Everyday Book,” but he had once been a hardened unbeliever. When sovereign grace had conquered him, he wrote:

The proudest heart that ever beat

Hath been subdued in me;

The wildest will that ever rose

To scorn Thy cause and aid Thy foes

Is quell'd my Lord, by Thee.

Thy will, and not my will be done,

My heart be ever Thine;

Confessing Thee the mighty Word,

My Saviour Christ, my God, my Lord,

Thy cross shall be my sign.

The Lord can give repentance to the most unlikely people, turning lions into lambs and ravens into doves. Let us look to Him to work this great change in us. Without doubt, thinking about the death of Christ is one of the surest and quickest ways to gain repentance. Do not sit down and try to pump repentance up from the dry well of corrupt nature. It goes against the very laws of the mind to suppose you can force your soul into that gracious state. Take your heart to Him in prayer — He understands it — and say, “Lord, cleanse it. Lord, renew it. Lord, work repentance in it.” The more you try to produce feelings of penitence in yourself, the more disappointed you will be; but if you think, with faith, of Jesus dying for you, repentance will burst out. Meditate on the Lord pouring out His heart’s blood out of love for you. Set before your mind’s eye the agony and bloody sweat, the cross and passion; and as you do, He who bore all this grief will look at you, and with that look He will do for you what He did for Peter, so that you too will go out and weep bitterly. He who died for you can, by His gracious Spirit, make you die to sin; and He who has gone into glory on your behalf can draw your soul after Him, away from evil and toward holiness.

I will be content if I leave you with this one thought: do not look under the ice to find fire, and do not hope to find repentance in your own natural heart. Look to the Living One for life. Look to Jesus for everything you need between Hell’s gate and Heaven’s gate. Never look anywhere else for any part of what Jesus loves to give; but remember,

Christ is all.

fields.title: The Fear of Final Falling
fields.body_html:
A DARK FEAR haunts the minds of many who are coming to Christ: they are afraid they will not persevere to the end. I have heard the seeker say, “If I were to throw my soul on Jesus, perhaps I would still draw back into ruin after all. I have had good feelings before, and they have died away. My goodness has been like the morning cloud and the early dew. It came suddenly, lasted for a while, promised much, and then vanished.”

I believe this fear often brings about the very thing it fears. Some who were afraid to trust Christ for all time and for all eternity have failed because they had a temporary faith that never went far enough to save them. They set out trusting Jesus to some extent, but looking to themselves to keep going and persevere on the road to heaven. So they set out on the wrong footing, and, naturally enough, turned back before long. If we trust ourselves to keep holding on, we will not hold on. Even if we rest in Jesus for part of our salvation, we will fail if we trust ourselves for anything. No chain is stronger than its weakest link. If Jesus is our hope for everything except one thing, we will fail completely, because at that one point we will come to nothing. I have no doubt at all that a mistaken view of the perseverance of the saints has stopped many who were running well from persevering. What hindered them from continuing to run? They trusted themselves for the running, and so they stopped short. Beware of mixing even a little of self into the mortar you build with, or you will make it untempered mortar, and the stones will not hold together. If you look to Christ for your beginning, beware of looking to yourself for your ending. He is Alpha; make sure you make Him Omega too. If you begin in the Spirit, you must not hope to be made perfect by the flesh. Begin as you mean to go on, and go on as you began, and let the Lord be all in all to you. Oh, that God the Holy Spirit may give us a very clear idea of where the strength must come from that will keep us safe until the day of our Lord’s appearing!

Here is what Paul once said on this subject when he was writing to the Corinthians:

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Cor. 1:8, 9).

These words quietly admit a great need by telling us how it is supplied. Wherever the Lord makes provision, we can be quite sure there was a need for it, since the covenant of grace is not cluttered with anything superfluous. Golden shields hung in Solomon’s courts that were never used; but there are none like that in God’s armoury. Whatever God has provided, we will certainly need. Between now and the end of all things, every promise of God and every provision of the covenant of grace will be called into use. What the believing soul urgently needs is confirmation, continuance, final perseverance, preservation to the end. This is the great necessity of even the most advanced believers; for Paul was writing to the saints at Corinth, who were people of a high order, of whom he could say, “I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ.” People like that are the very ones who most surely feel that they need fresh grace every day if they are to hold on, hold out, and come through as conquerors at the last. If you were not saints, you would have no grace, and you would feel no need of more. But because you are people of God, you feel the daily demands of the spiritual life. A marble statue needs no food; but a living man is hungry and thirsty, and he rejoices that his bread and water are guaranteed to him, because otherwise he would certainly faint on the way. The believer’s own personal needs make it inevitable that he should draw every day from the great source of all supplies; for what could he do if he could not turn to his God?

This is true of the most gifted saints — of those people at Corinth who were enriched with all utterance and all knowledge. They needed to be confirmed to the end, or their gifts and achievements would turn out to be their ruin. If we had the tongues of men and of angels but did not receive fresh grace, where would we be? If we had every kind of experience, until we were fathers in the church — if we had been taught by God so that we understood all mysteries — we still could not live a single day without the divine life flowing into us from our Covenant Head. How could we hope to hold on for a single hour, let alone a lifetime, unless the Lord held us on? He who began the good work in us must carry it on until the day of Christ, or it will turn out a painful failure.

This great need arises very largely from ourselves. Some people have a painful fear that they will not persevere in grace because they know how fickle they are. Certain people are unstable by temperament. Some are naturally cautious, not to say stubborn; but others are just as naturally changeable and flighty. Like butterflies, they flit from flower to flower until they have visited all the beauties of the garden, and settle on none of them. They never stay long enough in one place to do any good — not even in their business or their studies. People like this may well be afraid that ten, twenty, thirty, forty, perhaps fifty years of continual spiritual watchfulness will be far too much for them. We see people joining first one church and then another, until they have gone all round the compass. They are everything by turns and nothing for long. There is that within our hearts which should keep us watchful and humble before God. If He does not confirm us, we are so weak that we will stumble and fall — not knocked over by an enemy, but by our own carelessness. Lord, be our strength. We are weakness itself.

Besides that, there is the weariness that comes with a long life. Our pace seems slower, but it is more useful and better sustained. I pray God that the energy of our youth may stay with us, so far as it is the energy of the Spirit and not merely the fizzing of proud flesh. Anyone who has been on the road to heaven for a long time finds there was good reason why his shoes were promised to be iron and brass, for the road is rough. He has discovered that there are Hills of Difficulty and Valleys of Humiliation; that there is a Valley of the Shadow of Death and, worse still, a Vanity Fair — and all of these have to be crossed. If there are Delectable Mountains (and, thank God, there are), there are also Castles of Despair, whose insides pilgrims have seen all too often. All things considered, those who hold out to the end on the way of holiness will be “men wondered at.”

We have been kept alive on the very edge of death. Our spiritual life has been a flame burning on in the middle of the sea, a stone that has stayed hanging in the air. It will amaze the universe to see us enter the pearly gate, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. We ought to be full of grateful wonder if we are kept for even an hour; and I trust we are.

Some of us are greatly indulged by God’s providence, but others have a hard fight of it. We begin our day with prayer, and we often hear the sound of holy songs in our homes; but many good people have hardly got up from their knees in the morning before they are greeted with blasphemy. They go out to work, and all day long they are distressed by filthy talk, like righteous Lot in Sodom. Can you even walk along the public streets without your ears being assaulted by foul language? The world is no friend to grace. The best we can do with this world is to get through it as quickly as we can, for we live in enemy country. A robber lurks behind every bush. Everywhere we need to travel with a “drawn sword” in our hand, or at least with the weapon called all-prayer always at our side; for we have to fight for every inch of our way. Make no mistake about this, or you will be rudely shaken out of your comfortable delusion. O God, help us, and confirm us to the end — or where will we be?

fields.title: Confirmation
fields.body_html:
I WANT YOU TO NOTICE the security Paul confidently expected for all the saints. He says, “Who shall confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is the kind of confirmation to be desired above everything. You see, it assumes that the people are in the right, and it proposes to confirm them in the right. It would be a terrible thing to confirm someone in ways of sin and error. Think of a confirmed drunkard, or a confirmed thief, or a confirmed liar. It would be a dreadful thing for anyone to be confirmed in unbelief and ungodliness. Divine confirmation can only be enjoyed by those to whom the grace of God has already been shown. It is the work of the Holy Ghost. He who gives faith strengthens and establishes it; He who kindles love in us keeps it alive and makes its flame grow. What the good Spirit teaches us at first, He makes us know more clearly and certainly by further teaching. Holy acts are confirmed until they become habits, and holy feelings are confirmed until they become settled states. Experience and practice confirm our beliefs and our resolutions. Our joys and our sorrows, our successes and our failures, are all made holy to serve this same purpose — just as a tree is helped to root itself by both the gentle showers and the rough winds. The mind is taught, and as its knowledge grows, it gathers reasons for persevering on the good way. The heart is comforted, and so it is made to cling more closely to the comforting truth. The grip grows tighter, the step grows firmer, and the person himself becomes more solid and substantial.

This is not merely natural growth; it is as distinct a work of the Spirit as conversion is. The Lord will certainly give it to those who are relying on Him for eternal life. By His inner working He will save us from being “unstable as water,” and cause us to be rooted and grounded. This building us up into Christ Jesus, and causing us to remain in Him, is part of the way He saves us. Dear reader, you may look for this every day, and you will not be disappointed. He whom you trust will make you like a tree planted by the rivers of waters, kept so well that even your leaf will not wither.

What a strength a confirmed Christian is to a church! He is a comfort to the sorrowful and a help to the weak. Wouldn’t you like to be like that? Confirmed believers are pillars in the house of our God. They are not carried away by every wind of doctrine, or overthrown by sudden temptation. They are a great support to others, and act as anchors when trouble comes to the church. You who are just beginning the holy life hardly dare hope you will become like them. But you need not fear; the good Lord will work in you as well as in them. One of these days you who are now a “babe” in Christ will be a “father” in the church. Hope for this great thing — but hope for it as a gift of grace, not as wages for work or the product of your own energy.

The inspired apostle Paul speaks of these people as those who will be confirmed to the end. He expected the grace of God to keep them personally to the end of their lives, or until the Lord Jesus comes. In fact, he expected that the whole church of God, in every place and in every age, would be kept to the end of this age, until the Lord Jesus comes as the Bridegroom to celebrate the wedding feast with His perfected Bride. All who are in Christ will be confirmed in Him until that glorious day. Has He not said, “Because I live ye shall live also”? He also said, “I give unto my sheep eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” He who has begun a good work in you will confirm it until the day of Christ. The work of grace in the soul is not a surface reform. The life planted in the new birth comes from a living and incorruptible seed, which liveth and abideth for ever. And God’s promises to believers are not temporary; for them to be fulfilled, the believer must keep on his way until he reaches endless glory. We are kept by the power of God, through faith unto salvation. “The righteous shall hold on his way.” Not as the result of their own merit or strength, but as a gift of free and undeserved favour, those who believe are “preserved in Christ Jesus.” Jesus will lose none of the sheep of His fold; no member of His Body will die; no gem of His treasure will be missing on the day He gathers up His jewels. Dear reader, the salvation received by faith is not something that lasts for months or years; for our Lord Jesus has “obtained eternal salvation for us,” and what is eternal cannot come to an end.

Paul also declares his expectation that the Corinthian saints would be “confirmed to the end blameless.” This blamelessness is a precious part of our being kept. To be kept holy is better than merely to be kept safe. It is a dreadful thing to see religious people blundering from one disgrace into another; they have not believed in our Lord’s power to make them blameless. The lives of some professing Christians are a series of stumbles; they are never quite down, yet they are seldom on their feet. This is not fitting for a believer. He is invited to walk with God, and by faith he can reach steady perseverance in holiness — and he ought to. The Lord is able not only to save us from hell but to keep us from falling. We do not have to give in to temptation. Is it not written, “Sin shall not have dominion over you”? The Lord is able to keep the feet of His saints, and He will do it if we trust Him to. We need not soil our clothes; by His grace we may keep them unspotted from the world. We are bound to do so, “for without holiness no man shall see the Lord.”

The apostle foretold for these believers what he would have us all seek after — that we may be preserved “blameless unto the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Revised Version has “unreproveable” instead of “blameless.” Perhaps a better rendering would be “unimpeachable.” God grant that on that last great day we may stand free from every charge, so that no one in the whole universe dares to challenge our claim to be the redeemed of the Lord. We have sins and weaknesses to grieve over, but these are not the kind of faults that would prove us to be outside of Christ. We will be clear of hypocrisy, deceit, hatred and delight in sin; for these would be fatal charges. In spite of our failings, the Holy Spirit can work in us a character that is spotless in the eyes of others; so that, like Daniel, we give accusing tongues no grounds for complaint except in the matter of our faith. Multitudes of godly men and women have lived lives so transparent and so consistent from start to finish that no one could speak against them. The Lord will be able to say of many a believer what He said of Job when Satan stood before Him: “Hast thou considered my servant, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God and escheweth evil?” This is what my reader must look for from the Lord’s hands. This is the triumph of the saints — to keep following the Lamb wherever He goes, holding on to our integrity as in the presence of the living God. May we never turn aside into crooked ways and give the enemy cause to blaspheme. Of the true believer it is written, “He keepeth himself, and that wicked one toucheth him not.” May that be written of us!

Friend, you who are just beginning the divine life, the Lord can give you a character beyond reproach. Even though you may have gone far into sin in your past life, the Lord can set you completely free from the power of old habits and make you an example of goodness. He can not only make you moral; He can make you hate every false way and pursue everything that is holy. Do not doubt it. The chief of sinners need not be one bit behind the purest of the saints. Believe for this, and according to your faith it will be done to you.

Oh, what a joy it will be to be found blameless on the day of judgment! We are right to join in singing that lovely hymn:

Bold shall I stand in that great day,
For who aught to my charge shall lay;
While through Thy blood absolved I am,
From sin's tremendous curse and shame?

What bliss it will be to have that fearless courage when heaven and earth flee away from the face of the Judge of all! This bliss will belong to everyone who looks only to the grace of God in Christ Jesus, and in that sacred strength wages continual war against all sin.

fields.title: Why Saints Persevere
fields.body_html:
WE HAVE ALREADY SEEN that the hope Paul held for the Corinthian brothers is full of comfort for those who tremble about their future. But why did he believe the brothers would be confirmed to the end?

I want you to notice that he gives his reasons. Here they are:

“God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 1:9).

The apostle does not say, “You are faithful.” Alas! Human faithfulness is a very unreliable thing; it is mere emptiness. He does not say, “You have faithful ministers to lead and guide you, so I trust you will be safe.” Oh no! If we are kept by people, we will be poorly kept. He puts it this way: “God is faithful.” If we are found faithful, it will be because God is faithful. The whole weight of our salvation must rest on the faithfulness of our covenant God. Everything hinges on this glorious attribute of God. We are as changeable as the wind, as frail as a spider’s web, as weak as water. No reliance can be placed on our natural qualities or our spiritual achievements; but God remains faithful. He is faithful in His love; with Him there is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. He is faithful to His purpose; He does not begin a work and then leave it unfinished. He is faithful in His relationships: as a Father He will not disown His children; as a Friend He will not deny His people; as a Creator He will not abandon the work of His own hands. He is faithful to His promises, and will never let a single one of them fail a single believer. He is faithful to His covenant, which He has made with us in Christ Jesus and sealed with the blood of His sacrifice. He is faithful to His Son, and will not let His precious blood be shed in vain. He is faithful to His people, to whom He has promised eternal life, and from whom He will not turn away.

This faithfulness of God is the foundation and cornerstone of our hope of final perseverance. The saints will persevere in holiness because God perseveres in grace. He keeps on blessing, and so believers keep on being blessed. He continues to keep His people, and so they continue to keep His commandments. This is good, solid ground to rest on, and it fits delightfully with the title of this little book, “All of Grace.” So it is free favour and infinite mercy that ring in the dawn of salvation, and the same sweet bells sound out melodiously through the whole day of grace.

You see, the only reasons for hoping that we will be confirmed to the end and found blameless at the last are found in our God; but in Him those reasons are wonderfully abundant.

They lie, first, in what God has done. He has gone so far in blessing us that it is impossible for Him to turn back. Paul reminds us that He has “called us into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ.” Has He called us? Then the call cannot be reversed; for “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” The Lord never turns back from the effective call of His grace. “Whom he called them he also justified, and whom he justified them he also glorified”: this is the unchanging rule of God’s dealings. There is a general call, of which it is said, “Many are called, but few are chosen”; but the call we are thinking of now is a different kind, one that signals special love and makes certain that we receive what we are called to. In such a case it is with the one who is called just as it was with Abraham’s descendants, of whom the Lord said, “I have called thee from the ends of the earth, and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away.”

That means into partnership with Jesus Christ, and I want you to think carefully about what this means. If you really have been called by divine grace, you have come into fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ, so that you are joint owner with Him in everything. From now on you are one with Him in the sight of the Most High. The Lord Jesus bore your sins in His own body on the tree, being made a curse for you; and at the same time He has become your righteousness, so that you are justified in Him. You are Christ’s, and Christ is yours. As Adam stood for his descendants, so Jesus stands for all who are in Him. As husband and wife are one, so Jesus is one with all who are united to Him by faith — one by a marriage union that can never be broken. God has called us into this union, this fellowship, this partnership, and by this very fact He has given us the sign and pledge that we will be confirmed to the end. If we were considered apart from Christ, we would be poor perishable units, soon broken up and swept away to destruction; but as one with Jesus we are made sharers in His nature and are given His immortal life. Dwell often on this partnership with the Son of God to which you have been called, for all your hope lies there. You can never be poor while Jesus is rich, since you are in one firm with Him. Need can never overtake you, since you are joint owner with Him who is Possessor of heaven and earth. You can never go bankrupt; for though one of the partners in the firm is as poor as a church mouse — utterly bankrupt in himself, unable to pay even a small part of his heavy debts — the other partner is unimaginably, inexhaustibly rich. In such a partnership you are lifted above hard times, the changes of the future, and the shock of the end of all things. The Lord has called you into the fellowship of His Son Jesus Christ, and by that act and deed He has put you in a place of unfailing safety.

If you really are a believer, you are one with Jesus, and so you are secure. Don’t you see that it must be so? If you really have been made one with Jesus by the irreversible act of God, you must be confirmed to the end, until the day of His appearing. Christ and the believing sinner are in the same boat: unless Jesus sinks, the believer will never drown. Jesus has brought His redeemed into such close connection with Himself that He would first have to be struck down, overcome and dishonoured before the least of those He has bought could be harmed. His name is at the head of the firm, and until it can be dishonoured, we are safe from all fear of failure.

So then, let us go forward with the greatest confidence into the unknown future, linked for ever with Jesus. If the people of the world should cry, “Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her Beloved?” we will gladly confess that we do lean on Jesus, and that we mean to lean on Him more and more. Our faithful God is an ever-flowing well of delight, and our fellowship with the Son of God is a full river of joy. Knowing these glorious things, we cannot be discouraged. No — instead we cry with the apostle, “Who shall separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord?”

fields.title: Close
fields.body_html:
IF MY READER has not followed me step by step as he read these pages, I am truly sorry. Reading a book is of little value unless the truths that pass before the mind are grasped, taken as one’s own, and carried through to their practical results. It is like seeing plenty of food in a shop and still going hungry because you have not actually eaten any. It is all in vain, dear reader, that you and I have met, unless you have actually taken hold of Christ Jesus, my Lord. For my part, I had a clear desire to do you good, and I have done my best toward that end. It pains me if I have not been able to help you, for I have longed for that privilege. I was thinking of you when I wrote this page, and I laid down my pen and solemnly knelt in prayer for everyone who would read it. I am firmly convinced that great numbers of readers will receive a blessing, even if you refuse to be one of them. But why should you refuse? If you do not want the rich blessing I would have brought you, at least do me the justice of admitting that the blame for your final fate will not lie at my door. When we two meet before the great white throne, you will not be able to accuse me of having wasted the attention you were kind enough to give me while you were reading my little book. God knows I wrote every line for your eternal good. Now, in spirit, I take you by the hand. I give you a firm grip. Do you feel my brotherly handclasp? There are tears in my eyes as I look at you and say: Why will you die? Won’t you give your soul a thought? Will you perish out of sheer carelessness? Oh, do not do it! Weigh these solemn matters, and make sure of eternity! Do not refuse Jesus — His love, His blood, His salvation. Why would you? Can you really do it?

I beg you,

Do not turn away from your Redeemer!

If, on the other hand, my prayers are heard, and you, my reader, have been led to trust the Lord Jesus and receive salvation by grace from Him, then hold fast always to this teaching and this way of living. Let Jesus be your all in all, and let free grace be the one track along which you live and move. There is no life like the life of someone who lives in the favour of God. Receiving everything as a free gift keeps the mind from self-righteous pride and from self-accusing despair. It makes the heart grow warm with grateful love, and so it creates a feeling in the soul that is infinitely more pleasing to God than anything that could ever come from slavish fear. Those who hope to be saved by trying to do their best know nothing of that glowing fervour, that holy warmth, that devout joy in God, which come with salvation freely given according to the grace of God. The slavish spirit of saving yourself is no match for the joyful spirit of adoption. There is more real virtue in the smallest stirring of faith than in all the straining of those enslaved to the law, or in all the weary machinery of devotees who would climb to heaven by rounds of ceremonies. Faith is spiritual, and God, who is a spirit, delights in it for that reason. Years of reciting prayers, going to church or chapel, ceremonies and performances, may be nothing but an abomination in the sight of Jehovah; but a single glance from the eye of true faith is spiritual, and so it is precious to Him. “The Father seeketh such to worship him.” Look first to the inner man and to what is spiritual, and the rest will follow in due course.

If you yourself are saved, be on the lookout for the souls of others. Your own heart will not thrive unless it is filled with an intense concern to bless your fellow men and women. The life of your soul lies in faith; its health lies in love. Anyone who does not long to lead others to Jesus has never been under the spell of love himself. Get to the Lord’s work — the work of love. Begin at home. Next, visit your neighbours. Bring light to the village or the street where you live. Scatter the word of the Lord wherever your hand can reach.

Reader, meet me in heaven! Do not go down to hell. There is no coming back from that place of misery. Why would you want to take the road of death when heaven’s gate stands open before you? Do not refuse the free pardon, the full salvation, that Jesus gives to all who trust Him. Do not hesitate and delay. You have had enough of making resolutions; now act. Believe in Jesus now, with full and immediate decision. Take with you words and come to your Lord today — this very day. Remember, O soul, it may be

now or never

with you. Let it be NOW; it would be horrible if it were never.

Again I urge you,

meet me in heaven.
